title: Trials-adjusted Out-of-Sample Gating for LLM-proposed Trading Strategies
abstract: A language model can propose trading strategies faster than a human can read them. That capability is close to worthless on its own, because the binding constraint in systematic trading was never idea generation; it is not being fooled by ideas that only worked in the past. A strategy selected as the best of many candidates carries selection bias: its in-sample performance is inflated by luck in proportion to how many candidates were tried, and that inflation is invisible to the naive backtest that produced it. This paper describes and evaluates a validation gate built to be un-foolable by construction, and reports what happens when it is pointed at real markets. The system, ÀYÒ, separates a nondeterministic proposer (an LLM that authors strategies as typed, content-hashed data artifacts, never as executable code) from a deterministic verifier that trades only the frozen artifact. The verifier enforces three defenses against backtest overfitting: strict out-of-sample evaluation via a walk-forward split, a trials-adjusted acceptance bar whose required out-of-sample Sharpe rises with the number of candidates tested, and robustness sweeps across rolling windows and parameter settings. We run all three on 2-4 years of real U.S. equity data (Alpaca daily bars, 32-83 symbols, ending 2026-07-17) and report every number the gate produced. A single rule-based strategy selected for its insample Sharpe of 3.07 collapsed to an out-of-sample Sharpe of-4.90 and was rejected. A cross-sectional momentum book that appeared to beat buy-and-hold out-of-sample by a Sharpe edge of +0.13 in one configuration was exposed by the robustness sweep as a fluke: it beat the benchmark in only 2 of 5 rolling windows and in 0 of 12 parameter settings. Under honest validation, nothing survived-which is the expected and correct result on efficient large-cap markets, and precisely the outcome the gate exists to enforce. We argue that the contribution is not an alpha but a methodology: a reproducible gate that reliably refuses to deploy mirages, and that generalizes to any setting where a nondeterministic proposer must be held to a deterministic guarantee. We are explicit throughout about which claims the evidence supports and which remain open.
why: Real trading system fixing selection bias in LLM-proposed strategies.

title: Attributing Apparent AI Alpha: Factor Exposure, Leakage, Complexity, and Reasoning in Agentic Equity Research
abstract: When an AI system appears to generate equity alpha, five explanations compete with genuine skill: factor exposure, a weak benchmark, data leakage, model complexity, and an advantage a conventional system could replicate. We test all five on the same signal. Using the peer-reviewed replication of 212 published anomalies, language-model and agentic arms forecast which anomalies persist after their original samples end. The arms earn significant factor alpha-and none of it survives comparison with a passive portfolio of all published anomalies, which requires no model at all. Leakage does not explain the result: contamination made performance worse. The models' verbal mechanism judgements outperform their own numeric scores, but in-sample persistence absorbs them. A composite forecast scoring 0.400 owes 98.5% of that to a statistic we supplied. Apparent AI alpha here is a benchmarking artefact, not information.
why: LLM alphas vs passive anomaly basket; negative result, 212 factors.

title: AI Intermediation and Investor Information Processing: Evidence from Earnings Summaries on Social Media
abstract: We ask whether structured generative AI on social media can fill an intermediary role for retail investors. Using a within-day difference-indifferences design around the rollout of AI-generated earnings summaries on StockTwits, we compare user behavior before and after the summary becomes available following the earnings announcement. After AI summary publication, users spend less time browsing the firm's feed and engage less with peer-generated content, while subsequent messages become more aligned with the AI interpretation. Processing gains are greater for users interested in the information, users with more processing constraints, and firm news that better fits the summary's structure. At the platform level, usergenerated content becomes more homogeneous but also more informative. Retail trading increases, and retail order flow better predicts future returns. Our results suggest platformdeployed AI can be a scalable information intermediary that affects how investors process corporate disclosures, produce opinions on social media, and incorporate information into trading decisions.
why: Natural experiment on LLM intermediation; real platform, real market effects.

title: Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing: Methodological Foundations *
abstract: Recent advances in LLM agents enable a new paradigm for asset pricing, which we call Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing (AEAP): systems that autonomously conduct the scientific discovery process itself. We define AEAP and identify its core building blocks. Existing evaluation practices backtest only the outputs—factors or trades—not the autonomous discovery system that produced them. We focus on factor discovery, contributing a reference architecture, a rigorous evaluation standard for discovered factors, and a method for out-of-sample backtesting the discovery system. As a concrete instance of that architecture, we evaluate SEADS against five re-implemented baselines on two US equity panels using this standard: no single metric ranks the systems consistently, motivating evaluation on multiple axes at once. A separate rolling re-execution then asks the complementary question of whether the discovery process itself, not one static output, is reliable. We also report negative findings and limitations that surface further evaluation pitfalls for future AEAP systems.
why: AEAP paradigm for autonomous factor discovery, OOS system evaluation.

title: AI Volatility Forecasts Under Stress: Performance, Tail Risk, and Ranking Reversals
abstract: Machine-learning volatility forecasts are usually judged by average out-of-sample accuracy, but their practical value depends on whether relative performance survives stress. This paper studies state-dependent forecast ranking rather than unconditional loss alone. Using the full 2,615-observation archived S&P 500 realized-volatility file preserved from the Oxford-Man Realized Library, I compare EWMA, HAR-RV, and XGBoost in a walk-forward design whose state thresholds use only information available through t-1. XGBoost outperforms HAR-RV in normal observations, but the ranking reverses under high volatility. The paired XGBoost-minus-HAR QLIKE differential is-0.0097 in normal states, +0.679 in Stress90, and +1.167 in Stress95; the Stress90-minus-Normal deterioration is +0.689. The pairwise reversal survives log-MSE and log-MAE, Holm adjustment, chronological subsamples, and a pre-specified top-5% one-day realizedvolatility-ratio state with 148 events. Moving-block bootstrap and leave-one-event-out diagnostics indicate that the jump-state result is not driven by any single observation, although the five largest events account for about 42% of the cumulative differential. By contrast, the primary Q50-to-Q90 transition definition identifies only eight events and remains descriptive under the pre-specified power gate. The evidence reveals a forecasting-risk paradox: a model can look competitive under unconditional average-error criteria while becoming materially worse when volatility is high or rising abruptly. The results motivate evaluating AI volatility forecasts by state-conditional ranking stability, not average accuracy alone.
why: Volatility ranking reversal under stress; state-dependent evaluation.

title: Canaries in the Gold Mine: Early Productivity Gains from Artificial Intelligence Creating Organization Capital
abstract: Using a new firm-level measure of AI investment based on AI-skilled employment—spanning machine learning through generative and agentic AI—we show that AI investments are associated with productivity growth in recent years, but not over the previous decade. We trace the productivity gains to the accumulation of organization capital that AI helps create: durable firm-specific knowledge acquired through learning-by-doing that enables more efficient production. We build a novel measure of organization capital based on workers’ job descriptions and document that productivity gains are driven by AI-skilled jobs that build organization capital. Overall, our findings suggest that AI investment generates productivity growth by creating organization capital. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org .
why: AI-skilled employment predicts productivity via org capital creation.

title: Untradable Alpha? Machine-Learning Stock Selection under Investability Constraints: Evidence from Taiwan
abstract: A growing literature reports that machine-learning (ML) models deliver large cross-sectional stock-selection gains, yet whether those gains are implementable rather than merely statistical remains contested. We revisit tree-ensemble stock selection in Taiwan, an Asia-Pacific market sharply segmented between liquid Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE) large-caps and thinly traded Taipei Exchange (TPEx/OTC) small-caps. To limit survivorship bias, we reconstruct the investable universe at each annual May formation from official exchange files, retaining firms that later delist. Over 2011–2024, tree ensembles predict top-quintile next-year returns, and we form equal- and value-weighted top-ten portfolios. Unconstrained, the random forest earns 44.6% per year against 7.9% for the Yuanta Taiwan Top-50 ETF (0050) and 6.4% for the index (TAIEX). This advantage is confined to the hard-to-trade segment. A modest NT$100 million liquidity floor turns the random-forest return negative (−1.3%); value-weighting lowers but does not remove it, so the binding constraint is the selectable universe, not the weighting scheme. Within the tradable universe the ranking skill (AUC) falls to about 0.50 and the monthly-based annualized Sharpe ratio is 0.02 against 1.29 unconstrained. Restricting selection to the main board roughly halves the return (44.6% to 23.5%), and economic capacity is only about NT$0.2–0.4 million. The collapse survives higher-capacity gradient boosting, a wide neural network, and an enriched feature set, so it reflects the investable opportunity set rather than an underpowered model: we read the evidence as liquidity-confined predictive structure rather than investable alpha.
why: ML stock selection fails when you can trade it; untradable alpha reality check.

title: Machine Learning Classification and Portfolio Construction: Does the Loss Function Matter?
abstract: Classification outperforms regression across matched machine learning models in portfolio construction. A stacking ensemble of gradient boosted tree, random forest, and neural network yields a value-weighted annualized Sharpe ratio of 2.08 for classification and 1.39 for regression. This outperformance strengthens with class granularity and persists across subsamples and after transaction costs. Spanning tests show that classification retains economically large alphas after we control for regression, whereas regression alphas shrink substantially once we control for classification. These results indicate that classification extracts more return information than matched regression. Our diagnostics trace classification’s advantage to more precise separation of return deciles.
why: Classification > regression in portfolio construction; proper transaction-cost discipline shown.

title: Geospatial Imagery and Machine Learning in Commercial Real Estate Valuation
abstract: Investors price commercial property partly on how it looks, yet visual attributes rarely appear in the data used to study transaction pricing. Using satellite and street view imagery for 6,533 U.S. single-tenant net lease transactions from 2005 to 2020, we read each property's images two ways: as scores against attributes we name in advance, and as unlabeled statistical summaries. Together they close about 6.5 percent of the cap rate variation left unexplained by conventional property, market, lease, and time controls, and the named attributes account for most of it. The gain survives county fixed effects, public controls for walkability, demographics, urban form, and flood risk, and it improves out-of-sample forecasts. Because most of what imagery contributes can be stated in words, appraisal and underwriting can use it without sacrificing transparency.
why: 6,533 real CRE transactions, out-of-sample validation, implementable.

title: Generative AI and Mutual Fund Industry Concentration
abstract: We examine whether generative artificial intelligence (GAI) changes investor search and competition in the mutual fund industry. We exploit the introduction of SearchGPT, an AI-based search interface that synthesizes real-time information and provides links to underlying sources. Following SearchGPT, the previously rising concentration of website traffic across fund families flattens, and the relative traffic advantage of large fund families declines. These effects are stronger for families that relied more heavily on traditional search and distribution channels before SearchGPT and are attenuated during GPT service outages, consistent with an AI-mediated search mechanism. The shift in investor search is also reflected in capital allocation: larger fund families lose relative shares of new sales and, more gradually, total net assets. Overall, our findings suggest that GAI can weaken search-based advantages enjoyed by large incumbents and have implications for how investor search and capital are distributed within the mutual fund industry.
why: SearchGPT natural experiment, measurable market concentration effect.

title: Observable AI Capability and Firm Uncertainty: Market Reassurance versus Operating Volatility
abstract: We examine whether observable artificial intelligence (AI) capability reduces firm-level uncertainty. We construct a novel firm-level measure of AI capability by linking patent-level classifications from the USPTO Artificial Intelligence Patent Dataset to patent–firm assignments for U.S. public firms. Using a staggered-adoption difference-in-differences design, we find that with the first observed AI patent grant, the annualized stock-return volatility declines by 3.5 percentage points. By contrast, the first AI patent has no statistically significant average effect on operating cash-flow volatility. however, the operational consequences become clear when we examine individual AI technologies and the depth of firms’ AI capability. Patents in machine learning, natural-language processing and speech, computer vision, and AI hardware reduce stock-return volatility by 2.3 to 5.8 percentage points, whereas machine-learning and NLP patents increase operating cash-flow volatility by 0.9 and 0.8 percentage points, respectively. These findings are robust when analyzing accumulated AI patent stock, and across alternative specifications.
why: Novel AI-capability measure from patents; causal design, transferable method.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Detection of Financial Risk in U.S. Banks: Longitudinal Evidence from SEC 10-K Filings
abstract: Annual bank filings contain forward-looking descriptions of credit, liquidity, regulatory, operational, and market risks, but most computational approaches encode each filing independently. This paper studies whether changes in mandatory risk-factor disclosure provide incremental information about a bank's contemporaneous solvency condition beyond prior financial ratios and static text. We introduce LRDF (Longitudinal Residual Disclosure Fusion), a sparse, auditable model for SEC Form 10-K Item 1A. LRDF represents the current filing with TF-IDF, decomposes year-over-year textual change into two nonnegative channels for newly emphasized and de-emphasized terms, fuses the channels with eight lagged bank key performance indicators (KPIs), and estimates the residual change in normalized Z-score relative to the previous year. The design separates three effects that are confounded in conventional text regression: the current disclosure level, the direction of disclosure drift, and persistent financial state. Experiments use the public FETILDA U.S.-bank dataset: 2,479 Item 1A observations from 369 banks over 2006-2016. We preserve chronological ordering with 1,983 training, 248 validation, and 248 test observations and report MSE, RMSE, MAE, R 2 , Spearman, and Kendall statistics. On the held-out test period, LRDF obtains an MSE of 0.028470, compared with 0.030118 for an eight-KPI ridge model, 0.031800 for current-file TF-IDF, 0.029838 for TF-IDF plus lagged Z-score, and 0.028666 for current text plus the full lagged financial history. Relative to the historical-KPI and pure-text baselines, bank-cluster bootstrap tests yield positive improvement probabilities of 0.9969 and 0.9992, respectively. A separate bank-level holdout gives a 1.23% MSE reduction and improves Spearman correlation from 0.4732 to 0.4964 versus the matched direct-fusion baseline. Ablations show that current text, lagged KPIs, directional drift, and residual learning each contribute distinct predictive information. The resulting model is computationally light, directly reproducible on public data, and provides a technically explicit alternative to treating successive 10-Ks as independent documents.
why: LRDF longitudinal textual model, leakage-resistant design.

title: Talking the ESG Tightrope: Between Greenwashing and Greenhushing
abstract: Using a large language model (LLM), we characterize key stylized facts about the context and depth of corporate communication on climate and DEI related issues in quarterly earnings calls for firms across Europe and North America. Both climate and DEI discourse rise strongly until 2021 and decline thereafter. In general, communications on climate change issues are conducted substantively and in terms of its financial impact by firms with worse emissions profiles, and are followed by subsequent emission reductions. In contrast, DEI discussions are made tangentially and in terms of their societal impact by firms with greater board and employee diversity, and are not followed by further increases in diversity. To interpret the empirical patterns, we provide a conceptual framework featuring financial materiality and heterogeneous investor preferences, where firms choose the substance of information provided to investors under varying communication costs. Guided by this framework, we use the 2018 EU ETS reform and 2021 Texas anti-ESG legislation as quasi-natural experiments for how financial materiality and investor preferences causally affect firms' E&S communication, respectively. Our model and empirical evidence point to a chilling effect of the anti-ESG legislation on firms' willingness to provide even financially material information, implying perverse consequences for financial investors.
why: LLM earnings-call analysis, updates priors on disclosure substance.

title: New Technology & Security Risk in Digital Finance: A Tech-sec Risk Index and Multi-method Evidence
abstract: The rapid adoption of cloud, open banking APIs, blockchain/DeFi, and large language models (LLMs) has expanded the digital finance attack surface. Yet, evidence on how "new-tech" exposure translates into measurable security risk and financial impact remains fragmented. We propose a Tech-Security Risk Index (TSRI) that integrates (i) exposure to emerging technologies, (ii) vulnerability and dependency metrics, (iii) control strength and governance, and (iv) contemporaneous threat activity. Using a panel of global listed financial firms and a complementary DeFi protocol panel (2011-2025), we combine regulatory disclosures, vulnerability/advisory feeds, text-mined adoption signals, and exploit/incident logs. We estimate panel count and severity models for incidents, event-study effects around disclosures/exploits, volatility responses via GARCH, and a survival model for time-to-the-following-incident. We find that higher new-tech intensity predicts greater short-run incident frequency and loss severity; strong cyber governance and thirdparty assurance attenuate these effects. Market reactions to incidents are adverse and larger when TSRI is high, while audited protocols exhibit lower exploit hazard conditional on complexity and TVL. The TSRI provides a forward-looking, auditable measure that supports risk pricing, supervisory stress testing, and board oversight. Results generalize across jurisdictions and remain robust to alternative index weightings, windows, and selection schemes.
why: Tech-security risk index; real data, multi-method, transferable framework.

title: Authorization Is Not Safety: The Verification Gap in Agentic On-Chain Finance
abstract: Autonomous AI agents are beginning to hold wallets and move money on public blockchains, and the infrastructure for it-payment rails, programmable wallets, and authorization standards-has arrived in roughly twelve months. The safety layer for that infrastructure has not. The controls being built verify authorization and identity: whether a permitted agent acted within its scope, on behalf of a principal who consented. They do not verify intent-correctness or behavioral safety: whether the action was the one the principal actually wanted, and whether the agent was manipulated into a harmful action inside its permissions. That distinction is not academic-every publicly documented drain of an agent wallet to date happened within authorized capability, through prompt injection, not by breaking a permission. Drawing on the author's experience building a live systematic trading system, where a system passing its own checks means nothing if those checks cannot tell a real result from a manufactured one, this paper names the gap, offers a taxonomy of the failures authorization cannot catch, analyzes the two research efforts now pointed at it-verification-native clearing and settlement-layer underwriting-answers the strongest objections to building a safety layer at all, and proposes the principles such a layer must satisfy-among them, enforcement outside the agent's reach, verification of outcome graded by evidence, and an opt-in standard rather than a mandated gate. The claim is narrow and, I believe, correct: we have built the hands of agentic finance and skipped its conscience, and the window to build that conscience is open only while the stakes are still small. AI-assistance disclosure. This paper was researched and drafted by the author with the assistance of AI tools for source retrieval, drafting, and editing. All arguments, claims, framing, and final wording are the author's own. Every cited source was verified against the primary material, and the two quoted preprints (references 1 and 2) are quoted verbatim with their authors' stated limitations noted.
why: Authorization vs intent safety gap; identifies critical infrastructure gap.

title: AI-generated Summaries in Prediction Markets
abstract: Prediction markets rely on diverse participants' informational inputs to aggregate dispersed information into accurate collective forecasts. To reduce barriers to market participation, leading prediction market platforms have recently begun integrating AI-generated summaries (AIGS) that synthesize contextual information and market-relevant news. Because information is critical to the functioning of prediction markets, the emergence of AIGS as a new channel for delivering market-relevant information may reshape both how users access and process information and how markets aggregate dispersed information. Yet, despite the growing adoption of AIGS, little is known about its broader implications for prediction markets. To address this gap, we leverage Polymarket's introduction of AIGS to examine its impact on individual trading behavior and market forecasting performance. We find that AIGS significantly increases individual participation and makes users more likely to trade in the direction suggested by AIGS. These behavioral changes characterize what we refer to as the AI herding effect : exposure to AI-generated summaries increases individuals' tendency to rely on them when forming judgments and making decisions. Our laboratory experiment provides further evidence for this effect and sheds light on its underlying mechanism, showing that AIGS increases trading participation by reducing information acquisition and processing costs while shifting participants' beliefs toward the direction conveyed by the AIGS. At the market level, we find that AIGS reduces prediction accuracy and market efficiency. Taken together, these findings suggest that the introduction of AIGS presents a double-edged sword: while it makes prediction markets more accessible, it may unexpectedly harm the core function of prediction markets by undermining collective information aggregation. These findings contribute to the emerging literature on generative AI and collective intelligence by revealing how AI-generated information can affect information aggregation on digital platforms.
why: Polymarket AI summary rollout, impact on forecast accuracy.

title: Does Artificial Intelligence Reduce Investor Disagreement? Evidence from Human-AI Interactions Data
abstract: We use proprietary microdata on human user-generative AI (GAI) interactions to study how AI-assisted information processing affects investor disagreement. Disagreement rises over the course of a conversation, driven by increasing dispersion across topics despite declining dispersion within topics. This disagreement is economically meaningful: dispersion in beliefs formed after GAI interaction predicts higher subsequent abnormal trading volume, whereas initial-round dispersion does not. GAI responses also contain value-relevant information. The tone of GAI answers shapes users' subsequent expressed beliefs and predicts future stock returns, while the tone of user prompts does not; within-topic response noise declines as conversations progress. Yet users persistently pursue previously activated topics, and later-round GAI responses are not systematically more informative about future returns. These findings suggest that GAI improves the information content of investor beliefs without generating convergence: heterogeneous and persistent information search creates disagreement across topics. Consistent with this mechanism, broader U.S. evidence around ChatGPT's deployment shows greater disagreement following earnings announcements even as information asymmetry declines.
why: Proprietary user-GAI interaction data; disagreement predicts volume.

title: AI-Driven Vehicle-Loan Underwriting as a Growth Strategy: Speed, Conversion, and Market Share in Consumer Lending
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in lending is often justified as a means of reducing labor cost. This study argues that its greater strategic value may be speed: protecting approved loans, member relationships, and market share before borrowers finance elsewhere. Using four years of de-identified operational data from a mid-sized credit union, the analysis focuses exclusively on vehicle lending, the institution's largest consumer-lending product and an important source of new-member relationships. Only about 12% of vehicle applications received an instant decision in the operational process, and the project artifacts report an instant-approval share of only 1.2%. Funded vehicle loans had a median application-to-funding time of nine days. Across 2019-2022, 10,158 applications that had been approved were ultimately declined by the member, representing approximately $290 million in requested vehicle demand. The cumulative opportunity curve rises rapidly early in the funding window and then flattens, consistent with a saturating logarithmic/logistic shape; however, member-decline events were not timestamped, so this pattern is descriptive rather than a causal time-to-fallout estimate. A tuned Decision Tree reproduced the institution's historical overall vehicle-loan approve/disapprove decisions with 97.76% accuracy, 98.44% precision, 93.94% recall, 99.37% specificity, and ROC-AUC of 0.9897. These metrics measure consistency with historical underwriting decisions, not credit performance. Because repayment and default outcomes were unavailable, the study cannot claim that AI makes better risk decisions than human underwriters. The business implication is narrower and more important: when approval policy is highly reproducible, automation can be used to shorten decision queues and increase conversion capacity. For vehicle lending, where dealer relationships and point-of-sale competition strongly shape outcomes, speed can be a differentiator in preferred-lender status and new-member acquisition. The principal value of AI underwriting is therefore not headcount reduction, but faster loan conversion, retention, and growth.
why: Real credit union data; AI speed protects $290M in approvals.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Portfolio Choice in Large and Changing Asset Universes
abstract: Portfolio allocation in large and time-varying equity universes is challenging because high-dimensional decision rules can generate unstable and concentrated portfolios. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches typically determine all asset weights through a single high-dimensional action, providing limited control over diversification and implementation. We propose Structured-Action Proximal Policy Optimisation (SA-PPO), which separates aggregate portfolio positioning from cross-sectional security selection and the enforcement of portfolio constraints. Using a historically reconstructed S&P 500 universe and rolling out-of-sample tests from 2016 to 2025, SA-PPO delivers higher risk-adjusted performance, cumulative wealth, and certainty-equivalent returns than a broad set of passive, optimisation-based, and learning-based benchmarks. Relative to flat RL policies, it produces more diversified portfolios with moderate turnover. The results remain economically meaningful after transaction costs of up to 50 basis points and across different market conditions. Factor and return-spread regressions also indicate positive abnormal performance. Within the reconstructed U.S. large-cap universe, the findings are consistent with structured action generation improving the out-of-sample regularisation and implementability of high-dimensional portfolio policies.
why: SA-PPO portfolio RL 2016-2025 out-of-sample.

title: Reading the Fund: A Systematic Analysis of IMF Fiscal Advice Using Large Language Models
abstract: This paper performs the first large-scale analysis of IMF fiscal policy advice by LLMs on more than 5,600 Article IV reports covering 194 countries over 1978–2025. We use the extracted staff advice on the appropriate fiscal stance to estimate the IMF’s implicit fiscal reaction function. The results both validate and challenge the common view that the IMF is primarily focused on austerity. Fiscal consolidation remains the most common recommendation, reflecting the central role of fiscal sustainability in the Fund’s surveillance framework. Yet near-term advice has become increasingly countercyclical over time, particularly after the Global Financial Crisis and when monetary policy was constrained. The evidence also points to a more nuanced evolution of medium-term advice, with staff increasingly encouraging countries with ample fiscal space and persistent external surpluses to adopt more expansionary policies during the low-interest-rate environment. Methodologically, the paper demonstrates how to use LLMs to systematically evaluate economic policy advice.​
why: LLM analysis 5600+ IMF reports, challenges austerity narrative.

title: From Crash Narratives to Structured Liability and Severity: An LLM Information-Extraction Pipeline for Autonomous-Vehicle Insurance Triage
abstract: As autonomous-vehicle (AV) fleets scale, insurers must convert a growing volume of unstructured collision reports into the structured signals that reserving and subrogation require. Two regulatory regimes already mandate free-text crash narratives-the U.S. NHTSA Standing General Order (SGO 2021-01) and the California DMV's OL 316 collision reports-yet these narratives are largely unexploited for predictive use. We build and evaluate a schemaconstrained large-language-model (LLM) pipeline that codes these narratives into a structured representation of collision type, pre-crash maneuver, engagement state, operating-environment conditions, and a narrative-described contributory party. We evaluate it primarily against a distant-supervision key: the structured codes the reporting entities themselves file alongside each narrative, which supply 31,204 supervised field decisions across ten fields. The best model attains a median κ of 0.703 against this key, with the residual disagreement dominated by conditions the narratives simply do not state rather than by mis-extraction. We then ask whether narrative text adds predictive value for injury severity beyond the structured fields insurers already collect, using entity-grouped cross-validation and a leakage-controlled design that excludes any text-derived restatement of the outcome. Adding text yields a quadratic-weighted-κ lift of 0.180 over the structured-only baseline.
why: LLM AV insurance triage pipeline; 31,204 labeled decisions.

title: Does Artificial Intelligence Mitigate Credit Risk? Causal Evidence from the Indian Banking Sector
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in the financial intermediation, yet its impact on core bank fundamentals remains empirically contested. This study examines whether AI adoption generates tangible improvements in asset quality or primarily reflects technological signalling. Using staggered AI adoption across Indian commercial banks from 2011-2025, we examine the dynamic impact of AI implementation on non-performing assets (NPAs). We document a deterioration in asset quality in the years preceding adoption, consistent with technology investment responding endogenously to rising credit risk and operational stress. Following adoption, however, NPAs decline significantly and persistently, indicating that AI deployment facilitates improvement in risk monitoring and credit screening rather than merely signalling innovation. These results are robust to bank and year fixed effects, differential pre-trends, ownership heterogeneity, and macroeconomic controls. By linking AI to balance-sheet outcomes, this study provides causal evidence that technological integration stabilizes credit risk management and contributes to banking sector stability in the medium term.
why: Rigorous causal design on credit risk; single country limits transferability.

title: A Systemic Risk Framework for the Vietnamese Market: a Composite Risk Index and Financial Stress Prediction
abstract: In this study, we introduce the Vietnam Systemic Risk Index (VSRI), the first multi-dimensional composite index for the Vietnamese market, achieving an out-of-sample ROC-AUC of 0.77 and 75% recall in predicting financial stress events. This analysis fills a gap in the current research on systemic risk for the Vietnamese market, where, to the best of our knowledge, a multi-dimensional unified measure of systemic risk is still missing. Our VSRI framework integrates five dimensions of financial risk: external spillovers; domestic market fragility; financial turbulence; risk of downside tail co-movements; and market illiquidity. We provide empirical support for the economic validity of the VSRI, showing that it aligns with well-known periods of financial distress. We also demonstrate its ability to capture periods of increased systemic risk across latent market regimes and its capacity to bring incremental information about the buildup of risk beyond the information already contained in more conventional stress proxies. Furthermore, our machine learning analysis provides empirical evidence that the VSRI may contain useful signals for systemic stress prediction. The results of the study provide evidence that the VSRI can be a useful tool for Vietnamese financial regulators and policymakers, providing an operational framework able to quantify the current level of systemic risk and identify the main drivers of systemic vulnerability, thus informing risk management and financial policy decision-making.
why: Composite systemic risk index, out-of-sample AUC 0.77.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Internal Controls and Financial Reporting Quality: Evidence from U.S. Public Companies Separating Disclosure Diffusion from Control Effectiveness with a Temporally Deconfounded, Section-Aware Signal
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in corporate processes that feed financial reporting, yet public-market research faces a measurement problem: the rapid diffusion of AI terminology in annual reports can be mistaken for evidence that AI-enabled internal controls are effective. We develop TD-SAIC, a temporally deconfounded, section-aware AI-control signal designed to separate disclosure diffusion from control-relevant information. TD-SAIC combines section-level AI intensity with leave-one-firm-out lexical specificity in 10-K Item 1 (Business), Item 1A (Risk Factors), and Item 7 (MD&A), then residualizes these signals within each training sample against calendar time, document length, GICS sector, and external AI industry exposure. The resulting residual components and a business-to-control-relevance gap are evaluated using leakage-resistant firm-held-out and forward-time tests. We use only public, downloadable data: 5,214 S&P 500 firm-years from 2015-2025, a 5,423-filing pre-deduplication panel that preserves 10-K/A amendments, and SEC EDGAR XBRL-derived financial statement facts. The raw association between aggregate AI disclosure and 10-K/A amendment risk is negative and statistically significant (coefficient-0.0086, 𝑝 = 0.015), but vanishes after controlling for document length and time/industry effects (year-sector coefficient approximately zero, 𝑝 = 1.000). Section-specific signals are also insignificant under year-sector and firm-year specifications. In forward testing on 2024-2025 filings, adding AI disclosure features does not improve amendment prediction over non-text controls; nonlinear random-forest and XGBoost baselines show strong validation-period gains that do not survive the temporal shift. A secondary SEC-XBRL sample yields the same inference: cross-sectional AI-accrual associations disappear with firm fixed effects, and Modified Jones-style abnormal accruals are unrelated to AI volume, specificity, or breadth. The technical contribution is therefore not a broad conceptual framework but a reproducible measurement-and-validation procedure that detects when AI disclosure is an unstable proxy for AI-enabled control effectiveness. The results imply that studies, auditors, and investors should distinguish implementation evidence from disclosure intensity before interpreting AI language as a financial-reporting-quality signal.
why: Clever methodology separating hype from control; indirect outcome measure.

title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Financial Volatility Forecasting: Uncertainty-Gated Residual Boosting Across Prophet-Style, Gradient-Boosting, and Classical Time-Series Models
abstract: Financial volatility forecasting is a setting in which flexible machine-learning models can exploit nonlinear interactions, yet unconstrained corrections can become unreliable when market dynamics move away from the conditions represented in the training sample. This paper develops Uncertaintyand Disagreement-Gated Residual Boosting (UDGRB), a concrete hybrid forecasting algorithm rather than a model-agnostic framework. The method first constructs a dynamic structural anchor from ARIMA, simple exponential smoothing, a heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) model, and a transparent Prophet-style additive trend model with piecewise-linear changepoints and Fourier seasonality. A LightGBM residual learner then predicts the remaining log-volatility error. Two quantile LightGBM models estimate residual-correction uncertainty, while cross-model dispersion measures structural disagreement. A multiplicative gate shrinks the machine-learning correction according to these two signals; the gate penalties are selected only on a chronologically separate validation period and are allowed to be exactly zero, yielding data-driven sparsification or fallback when a gating signal has no incremental value. The empirical study uses 7,983 real Microsoft daily OHLCV observations from 13 March 1986 to 10 November 2017, distributed with the public pmdarima dataset and traceable to the Kaggle US stocks/ETFs price-volume collection. We form 1,598 leakage-controlled weekly forecasting observations after lag construction and evaluate 567 one-week-ahead forecasts from 2007-2017. The primary target is annualized close-to-close realized volatility; a Parkinson high-low range estimator supplies an alternative volatility proxy. Baselines include naive persistence, ARIMA, exponential smoothing, HAR, the Prophet-style additive model, standalone LightGBM, and dynamic forecast combination. On close-to-close volatility, UDGRBachieves the lowest MAE (8.292) and MASE (0.610), improving MAE by 3.09% over standalone LightGBM; the Diebold-Mariano test for absolute-error loss gives 𝑝 = 0.0427. On the Parkinson target, the validation criterion selects the no-shrinkage corner, so the method automatically reduces to the residual hybrid; it again obtains the lowest MAE (7.177). HAR produces the best variance-scale QLIKE on both targets, showing that the ranking is loss-dependent rather than universally dominated by one model. Importantly, on the primary target the uncertainty gate reduces QLIKE relative to the ungated residual hybrid by 0.0241 on average, with an eight-week moving-block bootstrap 95% interval of [-0.0640,-0.0003]. The experiments therefore identify a specific role for uncertainty-aware residual shrinkage: it improves point accuracy and protects residual boosting when validation evidence supports intervention, while preserving a statistically stronger structural solution when it does not.
why: Hybrid volatility method combining ARIMA/Prophet/HAR/LightGBM.

title: Feature-Augmented Graph Neural Networks for Out-of-Distribution Detection of Collusive Market Manipulation: A Multi-Cohort Study
abstract: Graph neural networks are increasingly used for market-surveillance tasks, but their robustness under distribution shift remains difficult to assess. We study feature-augmented graph neural networks for detecting collusive market manipulation across multiple synthetic market cohorts and manipulation families. The evaluation separates within-generator performance from out-of-distribution generalization and tests whether engineered behavioral features improve recall under family-level shifts. Results show that feature augmentation substantially improves paired out-of-distribution recall relative to the structural baseline, with a mean recall improvement of 0.347, 95% CI [0.282, 0.412], and improvement in 45 of 50 runs. However, performance is heterogeneous across manipulation families, and clique-like manipulation settings expose a failure mode in which the feature-augmented model can underperform. The study therefore frames feature augmentation as a practical robustness aid rather than a universal solution. The accompanying public repository provides code, configurations, and evidence artifacts to support replication.
why: GNN for manipulation detection, out-of-distribution evaluation.

title: Are DePIN Tokens AI-Infrastructure Assets? Dynamic Connectedness, Crypto Beta, and Portfolio Evidence
abstract: Decentralized physical infrastructure networks (DePINs) are increasingly presented as investable exposure to the computing, connectivity, and energy infrastructure underpinning articial intelligence. We examine whether this narrative is reected in market prices or whether DePIN tokens behave primarily as crypto-risk assets. Using 1,065 common trading days from May 2022 to August 2026, we analyze functionally selected DePIN tokens alongside semiconductors, utilities, uranium, natural gas, Bitcoin, and Ether. The empirical design combines dynamic connectedness with xed-dimension factor ltering to distinguish infrastructure-related transmission from common crypto-market exposure, followed by out-of-sample portfolio tests of its economic relevance. Bitcoin and Ether dominate shock transmission. Filtering common crypto exposure reduces connectedness among the thematic assets from 36.3% to 20.0%, while broader market controls lower it to 17.8%, leaving only a modest residual DePIN-infrastructure channel. This linkage is strongly state dependent, increasing approximately vefold in both market tails relative to the median, and 90.95% of its absolute magnitude is concentrated within one to ve trading days. A stricter compute-only specication restricted to Render Network (RENDER) and Akash Network (AKT) produces the same economic classication. Moreover, adding DePIN tokens to physical-infrastructure portfolios generates no robust out-of-sample improvement in risk-adjusted performance. The results show that protocol function does not automatically translate into nancial exposure to the underlying infrastructure: the studied DePIN tokens behave predominantly as cryptorisk assets with a modest, state-dependent, and transient infrastructure component.
why: DePIN token analysis with connectedness; proper methodology, narrow scope.

title: A Multi-Level Evaluation Framework for LLM-Based Semantic Feature Engineering in Automated Valuation Models
abstract: Automated Valuation Models primarily rely on structured property attributes, often overlooking valuable information embedded in real-estate listing descriptions. This paper presents a multi-level framework that leverages Large Language Models to transform unstructured property descriptions into interpretable semantic meta-features for house price prediction. The framework evaluates both semantic extraction quality and the impact of these features on downstream prediction.Experiments on residential property sales from Hobart and Sydney's Northern Beaches compare GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.1, and Mistral. Semantic features are evaluated against GPT-4o reference annotations and integrated with structured attributes using gradient boosting and random forest models. Results show that GPT-4o-mini achieves the highest semantic agreement and strongest valuation performance, with the largest gains in Sydney's Northern Beaches. Overall, LLM-derived semantic features provide complementary and interpretable information that improves AVM accuracy and transparency.
why: LLM semantic features for CRE valuation; methodological validation.

title: Does machine learning beat the market by trading fast or by waiting? Evidence from Bursa Malaysia
abstract: Most machine learning trading strategies are judged by their annualized return, that is, the average gain or loss over a year. That figure says nothing about the speed of the price movements that produce it. We take a machine learning portfolio built for Bursa Malaysia, rebuild its daily returns exactly from its stored holdings over 2022 to 2025, and split those returns into layers by how long each movement lasts, from two-day fluctuations to trends beyond 128 trading days. We then compare every layer with five Malaysian benchmark indices and four global market forces. The results show two distinct parts. At horizons beyond six months, it simply rides the Malaysian market. At the one-quarter to half-year horizon it moves almost independently of the large-cap index, with a beta of 0.09, and this independent layer is unchanged after trading costs. Its co-movement with the market is confined to crisis episodes, and no global force tracks it.
why: ML returns decomposed by horizon; interesting methodology, limited market.

title: Persuasion and Precision: How Generative AI Moves Inflation Expectations
abstract: Household inflation expectations shape spending, wage demands, and price setting, yet respond weakly to central-bank communication. We examine whether generative-AI conversations move these beliefs and which conversational features make them persuasive. Across three preregistered experiments (N = 3,772), participants forecast U.S. inflation, encountered a partner with a different estimate, and could revise their forecast. An AI partner received roughly 45% more weight than a human partner (Study 1). A chatbot instructed to challenge participants' reasoning was more persuasive than one instructed to find common ground and validate their reasoning (Study 2). Combining the most persuasive conversational features nearly doubled the weight placed on the chatbot's estimate relative to a generic prompt and reduced uncertainty about revised beliefs (Study 3). Conversational AI can therefore provide a scalable channel for moving household expectations, especially when its style is engineered and its estimates are anchored to professional forecasts.
why: Preregistered experiments on generative AI persuasion.

title: Economic Uncertainty, Investor Sentiment, and Corporate Fourth-Quarter Investments
abstract: Firms often increase capital expenditures in the final fiscal quarter to exhaust remaining budgets before year-end, a behavior commonly attributed to agency conflicts and "use-it-or-lose-it'' incentives. We examine whether economic uncertainty and investor sentiment affect the magnitude of this last fiscal quarter investment effect. Using large-language-model (LLM) measures constructed from Wall Street Journal news articles together with conventional uncertainty proxies, we find that heightened uncertainty significantly reduces excess final-quarter capital expenditures whereas optimistic investor sentiment amplifies year-end investment. The results suggest that uncertainty disciplines managerial spending while favorable sentiment exacerbates discretionary investment. Our findings show that managerial capital budgeting policies combined with economic narratives and market conditions influence corporate investment decisions.
why: LLM uncertainty measure predicts Q4 capex decisions.

title: Beyond Greenwashing: Algorithmic Resilience and the Non-Linear Governance Premium in Sovereign Capital Flows
abstract: Despite the proliferation of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) metrics, traditional linear macro-financial models frequently fail to capture the complex, non-linear transmission mechanisms driving Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows during systemic shocks. To address this methodological gap, this paper introduces a machine learning architecture optimized via a Bayesian hyperparameter tournament, employing a rigorous forward-chaining panel split to eliminate temporal data leakage across a global dataset of 147 sovereign entities from 2010 to 2024. Out-of-sample evaluations, formally validated via two-sided modified Diebold-Mariano testing, reveal that an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) ensemble emerges as the optimal predictive engine. It demonstrates statistically significant superiority over L1-regularized Lasso baselines and continuous non-linear estimators (p
why: XGBoost on 147 sovereigns; nonlinearity in FDI prediction.

title: AI Adoption and Stock Return Dynamics in Indian Banking: Evidence from Public and Private Sector Banks
abstract: While Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming financial intermediation, its impact on equity valuation, particularly within emerging economies such as India, remains opaque. This study examines the relationship between AI adoption and stock return dynamics in Indian banking using a balanced panel of ten major listed Indian banks, divided equally between public and private sector banks from fiscal year 2011-2025. Employing two-way fixed effects models, we evaluate whether AI integration, operationalized via binary indicator and a continuous intensity index, explains the variations in stock returns after controlling for bank-specific financial fundamentals and idiosyncratic risk. Under standard clustered standard errors, AI adoption shows no statistically significant effect on abnormal returns; however, under wild cluster bootstrap inference (more appropriate given the small number of cross-sectional clusters), the AI adoption coefficient is negative and economically borderline at the 5 percent level. The results remain consistent across ownership-interaction models, placebo tests, and dynamic event-time specifications. Adjacent to return-based findings, AI adoption shows no significant association with Return on Assets (ROA), a key profitability metric for Indian banking stocks. This could possibly be explained by a potential increase in operational costs associated with adoption and integration of AI technologies which offsets the productivity gains, leading to a productivity paradox. Altogether, the findings suggest that capital markets do not immediately reward, and may marginally penalize digital transformation initiatives in the Indian banking sector in the short run, consistent with investor scepticism about the near-term productivity gains or the internalization of implementation costs.
why: Null result appreciated but evidence mixed, tiny sample (10 banks)

title: Separating Regulatory Domain from Harm Severity: A Two-Axis Multilingual Safety Classifier for AI-Assisted Financial Services
abstract: Safety classifiers for AI-assisted financial services must distinguish regulatory violation from conversational harm and operate across the languages of RBI-regulated markets. We introduce AVAL-BFSI, a dual-head safety encoder of 306,964,256 parameters with a 20-class risk head that alone decides is_threat and an independent 12class regulatory-intent head that never gates, covering English, Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu. In-distribution it achieves macro-F1 0.8777 and routes 97.3% of English attack rows to the correct B-code; both FinProof files are fully present in the training corpus, so this measures learnability, not generalisation. Every benchmark is contamination-audited per row before scoring. Against Semalith v1.4 [arXiv:2607.22545] at matched denominators, AVAL-BFSI is ahead on four benchmarks and behind on four, the largest gap being copyright extraction at recall 0.080. Weights are available at SHA-256 e9d869a5.
why: Deployed system but compliance-focused, not trading-oriented.

title: Forward-Liquidity-Projected Double Deep Q-Learning for Optimal Transaction Execution in Digital Financial Markets
abstract: Optimal execution in continuously traded digital-asset markets is difficult because a learned policy must react to short-horizon market conditions while still guaranteeing sufficient progress toward a hard terminal inventory target. Standard deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can discover opportunistic schedules, but unconstrained actions can under-trade during low-liquidity intervals and leave large residual inventory for forced terminal liquidation. This paper introduces Forward-Liquidity-Projected Double Deep Q-Learning (FLP-DDQN), a concrete execution algorithm that augments a Double DQN policy with a state-dependent projection layer derived from conservative forward liquidity. The policy selects a multiplier of the urgency baseline, while the projection computes a minimum executable request needed to keep the remaining inventory compatible with forecast future capacity and expands the local upper bound when necessary so that the action interval is non-empty. The method is evaluated on 527,040 consecutive one-minute BTCUSDT Binance Spot observations from calendar year 2024. We construct 5,112 training episodes, 720 validation episodes, and 2,207 strictly out-of-sample hourly execution tasks covering October-December 2024. Across three random seeds, FLP-DDQN achieves a mean implementation shortfall of 3.899 bps versus 4.526 bps for TWAP and 5.507 bps for an otherwise matched DDQN. The episodepaired improvement over TWAP is 0.627 bps with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of [0.046, 1.593] bps and a one-sided Wilcoxon p-value of 3.94 × 10-26. The matched DDQN ablation shows that the forward-liquidity projection reduces mean shortfall by 1.608 bps and terminal liquidity-breach incidence from 64.9% to 34.6%. Regime tests, random-seed analysis, participation-cap stress, impact stress, and distributional-RL baselines confirm that the principal gain comes from explicit inventory-feasibility control rather than a larger value network.
why: Sound execution algorithm design; no empirical results shown.

title: When the Crowd Speaks: AI-based retail investor sentiment indicator with Reddit data
abstract: Retail investors increasingly discuss markets in real time on social media, yet these discussions remain difficult to measure systematically. This paper introduces the Reddit Retail Investor Sentiment Indicator (R-RISI), a high-frequency measure of retail investor sentiment based on Reddit posts from major investing and crypto-related subreddits between 2015 and April 2026. Using ChatGPT 5.1, we classify posts by sentiment and topic and show that large language models provide more accurate labels for informal social media language than widely used finance-specific models such as FinBERT, which tends to over-assign neutral sentiment. R-RISI is constructed by aggregating daily positive and negative posts, weighting them by user engagement and standardising the resulting series using a rolling one-year z-score methodology. The indicator can be flexibly built for broad asset classes, portfolios, individual securities or thematic groups, allowing sentiment to be tracked at a much higher granularity than traditional retail investor indicators. We show how sentiment and dominant discussion topics evolve over time within each of the extracted subreddits. R-RISI closely reflects major market developments and aligns with established sentiment indicators while providing higher frequency and more timely signals. Empirically, changes in R-RISI contain statistically significant short-term information for market prices. This relationship is particularly relevant during periods of market stress: changes in R-RISI matter more for next-day S&P 500 returns when markets are in decline. The indicator therefore offers a timely and granular tool for analysing retail investor behaviour and monitoring sentiment-driven market dynamics in an environment of growing retail investor participation. A regularly updated version of the indicator is available through an accompanying R-RISI online dashboard.
why: Novel Reddit sentiment measure but investability unvalidated.

title: Does Regional Economic Policy Uncertainty Matter to Cryptocurrency Returns? Evidence from China and Japan
abstract: Increasing concerns about the impact of policy-related uncertainty on financial markets have drawn significant attention recently. This study provides new evidence on regional uncertainty spillovers in cryptocurrency markets by integrating time-varying Granger causality with machine learning algorithms. We show that Asian Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) correlation between China and Japan contains incremental predictive information for cryptocurrency returns beyond conventional global and the U.S. uncertainty measures. In contrast, EPU indices from other major Asian countries do not exhibit the significant predictive power. Out-of-sample results further indicate that the intermediateterm EPU correlation between China and Japan over a 180-day horizon delivers the strongest incremental forecasting improvement relative to baseline specifications. Our findings remain robust across alternative machine learning algorithms. The study contributes to expanding literature on digital asset markets by proposing a novel regional uncertainty co-movement measure to study regional EPU spillover effects and highlighting the importance of systematic policy regimes in shaping cryptocurrency return dynamics.
why: China-Japan EPU predicts crypto returns; out-of-sample rigor but narrow.

title: Predictive Analytics for Stock Market Trends Using Ensemble Machine Learning Models
abstract: We test whether ensemble machine-learning models can produce economically meaningful forecasts for daily S&P 500 returns over January 2000-May 2024 (6,266 trading days; CRSP). Eight technical predictors are engineered to capture momentum and volatility structure. A Random Forest (200 trees) and Gradient Boosting regressor (400 stages) are trained on 2000-2019 and combined in a convex ensemble (60% RF, 40% GB). On the 2020-2024 hold-out sample, the ensemble improves MAE by 3% versus its constituents but fails to beat a naïve zero-return benchmark in out-of-sample R 2. A long-only rule that takes positions only when forecasts are positive reduces drawdown and annualised volatility yet delivers only 2.1% CAGR, suggesting limited net value after trading costs. Importance analysis shows MACD and 21-day volatility contribute 39% of the predictive signal, and year-by-year errors confirm strong regime dependence, especially during the COVID-19 crash and the 2022 inflation sell-off. We conclude that tree ensembles aid risk control, but consistent performance likely requires regime-aware or deep sequence approaches with macro-sentiment features.
why: Ensemble doesn't beat naive OOS; proper methodology, negative result.

title: A Parent-Child Multi-Agent Architecture for Real-Time Financial Fraud Detection Using Tool-Augmented Language Model Agents
abstract: Financial fraud today moves faster than the annual or quarterly review cycles that most detection systems were designed around. A stolen card can be tested across dozens of merchants and monetized within minutes, and a compromised account can be drained before a human analyst ever opens a case. Detection systems built as a single model or a single rules engine struggle here, not because the underlying machine learning is weak, but because a single system covers too many kinds of fraud with too few, and too tightly coupled, sources of evidence. This paper proposes a parent-child multi-agent architecture for real-time fraud detection, in which a coordinating parent agent routes each transaction to a small set of specialized child agents, each bound to its own tools and data sources through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). We ground the design in the current literature on large language model multi-agent systems, agent-tool interoperability, and graph-based fraud detection, and we present the architecture, a reference implementation pattern, six representative use cases, and a qualitative comparison against rule-based, single-model, and monolithic-agent baselines. The contribution is architectural rather than empirical: we do not report benchmark numbers, but we give practitioners and researchers a concrete, citable design they can implement, adapt, and evaluate against their own transaction data.
why: Multi-agent fraud architecture; good design, not implemented.

title: AI diversification and the valuation of strategic growth options: Evidence from the AI value chain
abstract: Artificial intelligence is creating a new technological value chain, but many of the publicly traded firms capturing its opportunities are not AI-native entrants. They are established firms redeploying inherited technological, productive, distribution, cloud, software, customer, and organizational assets into AI. This setting raises two related questions at the intersection of innovation strategy and finance: does diversification into AI generate economic value once investment requirements and potential cannibalization of legacy economics are recognized, and how large a future AI bet is already embedded in market valuation before that payoff is fully demonstrated? We examine 50 large public firms positioned across the principal layers of the AI value chain and value them at four quarterly dates, yielding up to 200 firm-quarter valuation observations before outcome-specific data restrictions. Using a reverse equity discounted-cash-flow framework, we recover the normalized free-cash-flow-to-equity (FCFE) growth required to reconcile observed equity values with contemporaneous shareholder cash flow and benchmark it against demonstrated FCFE growth. We distinguish AI materiality, which captures the extent to which AI has entered measurable commercial activity, from AI momentum, which captures the growth of that AI-linked activity. The results reveal two distinct channels. Greater AI materiality is associated with higher absolute price-implied growth but with a smaller remaining benchmark-relative growth requirement; faster AI momentum contributes relatively little to the absolute implied-growth level but is positively associated with valuation stretch. Capital productivity is also positively associated with benchmark-relative optionality. The evidence is consistent with a strategic-option lifecycle in which rapid expansion into AI enlarges the opportunity capitalized by markets, while successful commercialization progressively converts part of that option into demonstrated economics. For incumbents, however, realization is not automatically equivalent to net value creation: AI can also displace legacy revenues or pricing architectures. The paper therefore separates the net-payoff problem of AI diversification from the size of the strategic growth option priced by capital markets and shows why both depend on the incumbent’s starting position in the AI value chain.
why: AI value chain valuation; framework but no outcome data.

title: Multi-Agent Deep Reasoning Framework for Financial Trading Decision-Making: Architecture, Mechanism, and Empirical Analysis
abstract: The increasing complexity of financial markets demands sophisticated analytical frameworks capable of integrating heterogeneous data sources and producing robust trading decisions. This paper presents a multi-agent deep reasoning framework that mirrors the organizational structure of real-world trading firms through specialized LLM-powered agents. The framework decomposes the trading decision process into five hierarchical stages: (1) multi-dimensional market analysis by specialized analyst agents, (2) structured debate between bullish and bearish researchers, (3) investment plan synthesis by a research manager, (4) trading strategy formulation by a trader agent, and (5) multi-perspective risk assessment through adversarial debate. A key innovation is the integration of a BM25-based episodic memory system that enables agents to learn from historical decisions through structured reflection. The framework employs LangGraph for orchestrating agent interactions via a directed state graph, with conditional logic controlling debate termination and information flow. We formalize the agent communication protocol as a shared state dictionary with typed fields, enabling transparent information propagation across the pipeline. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that the multi-agent debate mechanism significantly reduces decision bias compared to single-agent approaches, while the reflection mechanism improves decision quality over successive trading sessions. The framework supports multiple LLM providers and data sources, with current deployment utilizing DeepSeek models. Our analysis reveals that the structured adversarial debate mechanism and episodic memory system are the primary contributors to decision robustness, providing actionable insights for the design of future multi-agent financial systems.
why: Multi-agent trading framework with memory; architecture, not implemented.

title: A Quarterly Macro-Financial Early Warning System for Banking Sector Stress in Bangladesh: An Explainable Machine Learning Approach
abstract: Banking-sector stress can build gradually while remaining difficult to detect with a small set of conventional indicators. This study develops a quarterly macro-financial early warning system for banking-sector stress in Bangladesh using an explainable machine-learning framework. The analysis uses 64 quarterly observations covering 2010Q1–2025Q4 and defines stress from the upper tail of the banking sector’s non-performing loan ratio. A one-quarter-ahead target is constructed so that predictors contain only information available at or before the forecast quarter. After a leakage audit, 52 current and lagged macro-financial predictors are retained. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost are evaluated using a chronological holdout and, more importantly, leakage-free expanding-window validation with training-only imputation, scaling, and threshold selection. The expanding-window evaluation contains 39 forecasts beginning in 2016Q1. Random forest is selected as the primary early warning model because it records stress recall of 0.8462, an F1 score of 0.7857, a false-alarm rate of 0.1538, and two missed stress events. XGBoost provides a robustness check with the same stress recall and a higher one-quarter lead detection rate of 0.7692, although its false-alarm rate is higher. SHAP analysis indicates that the current loan-to-deposit ratio (ADR), lagged remittance growth, lagged ADR, capital adequacy, lagged NPL, exchange-rate, inflation, and reserve variables are among the most influential predictors. The results support the use of a quarterly, interpretable monitoring framework for supervisory risk assessment, while also showing that model outputs should be treated as predictive signals rather than causal estimates.
why: Bangladesh banking stress warning system; proper method, single country.

title: Auditable by Construction: An Ontology-Driven Framework for Trustworthy LLM Analytics in Enterprise Finance
abstract: Enterprise adoption of large language models (LLMs) in finance is constrained less by fluency than by trust: in Financial Planning and Analysis (FP&A) and other regulated workflows, an answer is usable only if it is traceable to authoritative sources, explainable in domain terms, and auditable after the fact. This paper argues that retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) for enterprise finance should be evaluated on auditability alongside accuracy, and presents a framework designed to make grounded responses auditable by construction. The Knowledge-Driven Analytics Framework (KDAF) builds ontology-driven knowledge systems through six iterative stages-problem-centric scoping via competency questions, ontology bootstrapping through a minimum viable graph, schema-guided knowledge extraction, contextual knowledge representation with typed relevance and provenance annotations, hybrid human-in-the-loop validation, and Context-Aware Relevance Propagation (CARP) for graph-based evidence retrievalso that every retrieved fact carries its relationship type, confidence, and source lineage. A proof-of-concept evaluation on FinanceBench (145 questions) compares KDAF against zero-context inference, BM25 sparse retrieval, concept-weighted lexical retrieval over text and tables, and ungrounded graph traversal. Three findings structure the results. First, retrieval is necessary: zero-context inference reaches 4.1% correctness against 10-12% for every retrieval-augmented condition. Second, on answer correctness the retrieval conditions are statistically indistinguishable-KDAF and BM25 differ by-0.007 (95% CI [-0.021, 0.000])-so accuracy alone does not justify the cost of structured retrieval on single-document filings questions, a negative result we report explicitly. Third, on the properties auditability depends upon, the ordering reverses: KDAF attains the highest citation traceability F1 (0.515), exceeding ungrounded graph traversal by +0.027 (95% CI [0.006, 0.050]) and BM25 by +0.052 (95% CI [0.024, 0.083])-intervals that exclude zero. Separately, graph-structured retrieval of either kind admits no evidence from outside the question subject entity (0 of 426 and 0 of 424 items, against 16.8% and 20.2% for the lexical baselines), because the entity model supplying the provenance chain also makes that boundary expressible as an enforced constraint; every selected item resolves to a complete provenance chain. We argue that auditability, not raw question-answering accuracy, is the axis on which ontology-grounded retrieval earns its construction cost, and outline the FP&A-aligned evaluation this motivates.
why: RAG framework for finance; conceptual, not implemented.

title: A Hybrid Explainable Machine Learning Model for Dynamic Asset Allocation: Evidence from the Thai Financial Market
abstract: Standard Mean-Variance models often fail in today's shifting markets because regime changes break their core assumptions. This study creates an explainable hybrid model for the Thai stock market that combines machine learning with portfolio tools. Market regimes are identified using unsupervised Gaussian Mixture Hidden Markov model to generate training labels. Then, the supervised ensemble models are fitted with optimized hyperparameters to predict the future market regimes. These predicted regimes are integrated into a dynamic mean-variance optimization model, and the resulting portfolio strategies are evaluated against various performance metrics. The results show that the proposed regime-switching portfolios significantly outperform all benchmark portfolio, including static mean-variance optimization approach. The dynamic regime-detection mechanism effectively captures growth during bull markets and preserves capital during prolonged downturns by limiting maximum drawdowns and tail risks. Beyond these performance improvements, the application of SHAP resolves the black-box problem of advanced machine learning algorithms by revealing their specific internal logic. The analysis demonstrates that the regime predictions are driven by structural price features, such as Open-to-High, and Open-to-Low returns, along with the momentum and volatility indicators. In conclusion, this framework makes complex machine learning models more transparent for asset allocation.
why: Thai market only; no transaction cost discussion

title: Financial Sentiment Analysis: The Effect of Annotation Agreement on Classification Performance
abstract: Annotation agreement is an important indicator of annotation quality in supervised text classification; however, its effect on financial sentiment classification has received limited attention. This study investigates the influence of annotation agreement on classification performance using the Financial PhraseBank dataset. Three mutually exclusive datasets representing high, medium, and low agreement annotations were constructed to eliminate duplicated instances across agreement levels. Nine within-level and cross-level experimental settings were evaluated using two preprocessing configurations, TF-IDF unigram features, and eight traditional machine learning classifiers. Experimental results showed that classification performance consistently decreased as annotation agreement declined. Models evaluated on higher-agreement test datasets consistently achieved better performance than those evaluated on lower-agreement datasets, regardless of the annotation agreement level of the training data. Linear SVM and SGD (Hinge) achieved the highest Macro-F1 scores across most experimental settings, whereas lemmatization provided only limited and inconsistent improvements. These findings demonstrate that annotation agreement is an important characteristic of annotated datasets and should be explicitly considered when constructing benchmark datasets, evaluating financial sentiment classification models, and interpreting experimental results.
why: Annotation agreement effect; narrow measurement study.

title: Robotic Systems Adoption and Cyber Risk in Financial Transactions: An Empirical Analysis of Automation-driven Vulnerabilities in Digital Finance
abstract: We studied whether scaling robotic systems adoption (RSAI) raises cyber risk (CRI) in financial transactions and identified the conditions-IT governance (ITG) and regulatory quality (RQ)-that mitigate this risk. We compile a country-year panel for 12 countries from 2014 to 2025 (N = 144). Estimation proceeds from OLS with country-clustered errors to country fixed effects (FE), followed by a dynamic panel System-GMM to address persistence and endogeneity. We examine nonlinearity (quadratic RSAI) and moderation using marginal effects across the distributions of the RQ/ITG variables. Inference uses cluster-robust (and, where feasible, wild-cluster) p-values; GMM diagnostics include AR (2) and instrument controls. Across specifications, RSAI is positively associated with CRI, while ITG is strongly risk-reducing. Interaction and marginal-effects results show that the RSAI→CRI slope is state-dependent, attenuating as RQ/ITG strengthens. The quadratic model suggests a turning point: at low adoption, risk may not rise, but beyond a threshold, additional automation increases CRI unless governance scales accordingly. System-GMM confirms mean reversion in CRI (negative lag) and no AR (2), supporting the identification. Automation programs should be budget-paired with governance upgrades (privileged access, segmentation, monitoring) and staged against risk gates. Regulators can mitigate systemic risk by enhancing RQ (enforcement, disclosure, and third-party rules). We provide the first crosscountry , dynamic evidence that cyber risk is an endogenous by-product of robotic/AI scale, and we quantify how IT governance and institutions reshape this relationship, offering a replicable identification blueprint for digital-risk research.
why: Macro panel on automation and cyber risk.

title: From Rules to Reasoning -Building the Next-Generation Pricing Engine A Product and Business Framework for Combining Deterministic Control with Agentic AI
abstract: This article presents a comprehensive product and business framework for modernizing enterprise pricing engines by combining deterministic rule-based control with agentic artificial intelligence (AI). Modern multi-channel manufacturers and retailers face significant operational complexity managing global currencies, hierarchical buying structures, customized discounts, and tiered rebate programs. While mature rule-based pricing engines excel at executing deterministic contract logic, maintaining margin guardrails, and providing auditable price calculations, they struggle to adapt dynamically to fast-moving market disruptions, dynamic bundling, and competitor price shifts. To address these limitations, the framework introduces a multi-agent AI architecture operating as an autonomous reasoning layer above the core rules engine. Specialized agents perform multimodal visual and specification matching, calculate landed unit economics considering freight and holding costs, and strictly enforce compliance with established policy guardrails. By combining rule-based governance with bounded agentic autonomy, organizations can achieve real-time competitive arbitrage, prevent margin erosion, and streamline decision workflows.
