The framework emphasizes system governance, explainable pricing logic, and progressive rollout strategies moving from shadow execution to controlled autonomy to build commercial trust and maximize contribution margins across complex global selling environments.
why: Pricing engine framework; position paper.

title: Beyond Provenance: Dependency-aware Integrity Controls for AI-assisted Financial Decision Support
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in financial analysis and decision-support workflows, yet a decision-material conclusion can remain unreliable even when the underlying document is authentic and the extracted numerical value is correct. Failures may instead arise from entity mismatch, temporal leakage, incompatible reporting periods, currency or dimensional inconsistency, financial-semantic substitution, unrecorded runtime dependencies, obsolete policy application, or invalid decision authority. This paper introduces AICOS as a dependency-aware research architecture for financial decision integrity. The architecture represents decision-material evidence as financially typed objects, distinguishes evidence that is merely available from evidence actually consumed at runtime, and records version-bound dependency paths linking evidence, financial claims, computations, policy evaluations, recommendations, human authority, and final decision states. The architecture is evaluated through FDIB-1, a controlled Financial Decision Integrity Benchmark based on paired clean and mutated cases spanning evidence, temporal, semantic, dimensional, execution, policy, dependency, and authority failures. The proposed evaluation compares the full architecture against an ungoverned language-model condition, a provenance and traceability baseline, and a strong deterministic financial validator. The primary endpoint is Unsupported Critical Claim Rate (UCCR), complemented by Supported Claim Coverage, appropriate abstention, dependency-impact precision and recall, false-positive governance behavior, evidence-closure quality, and operational overhead. The study deliberately separates decision integrity from predictive accuracy, regulatory compliance, and economic outcome correctness. A positive result would therefore support only the bounded claim that the evaluated controls improve measured integrity properties under the tested tasks, mutations, system versions, and experimental conditions.
why: Decision integrity framework; conceptual, not implemented.

title: Generative AI, Net Productivity, and Firm Valuation: Evidence from Firm-Level Data
abstract: Generative AI is rapidly being integrated into firms’ production, R&D, marketing, and information-processing activities. A striking divergence has emerged in both the market and academic discourse regarding its economic impact: at the micro level, an expanding body of experimental evidence finds that Generative AI can substantially improve the speed and quality of specific tasks; yet when the analytical focus shifts from individuals and individual tasks to firms and even the broader economy, productivity has not experienced a commensurate surge matching the technological enthusiasm surrounding AI. For example, Noy and Zhang’s randomized experiment involving 453 professionals found that ChatGPT reduced task completion time by approximately 40% while increasing output quality by 18%. Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond, using data from 5,172 customer-support agents, found that AI assistance increased the number of issues resolved per hour by approximately 15%, with substantially larger gains among less-experienced workers. These findings are not difficult to understand. If an employee can complete coding, copywriting, information retrieval, or customer-service tasks more quickly, the employee’s task-level efficiency can indeed improve. Yet a firm is not simply the sum of its individual employees. To integrate AI into its production processes, a firm must also incur costs associated with model inference and computational capacity, system integration, employee training, human verification, organizational adjustment, and data security. Consequently, productivity gains at the task level do not necessarily translate into higher net productivity at the firm level, nor do they imply that shareholder value has been realized simultaneously. The issue becomes more complex at this point. Capital markets generally do not wait several years for firms to report their eventual productivity outcomes before incorporating technological developments into asset prices. As long as investors believe that a technology may alter future cash flows, equity prices may respond in advance. Generative AI may therefore generate two simultaneous effects: on the one hand, it genuinely improves the efficiency of certain tasks and employees; on the other hand, markets may already begin to revalue firms according to their exposure to AI, technological capabilities, and expectations regarding future economic benefits. This paper therefore examines the transmission process through which Generative AI moves from “task efficiency” to “firm-level net productivity” and ultimately to “market valuation.” More specifically, it asks: why do the micro-level productivity gains that have already been documented not necessarily translate contemporaneously into firm-level net productivity and market value?
why: Position paper on productivity paradox; no new evidence.

title: Identifying and Forecasting US Equity Market Regimes: An Unsupervised and Supervised Machine Learning Analysis of Bull and Bear Market States, 2010-2025 A Research Paper on Quantitative Finance and Market Regime Classification
abstract: This paper investigates whether unsupervised machine learning can identify economically meaningful regimes in the US equity market and whether such regimes provide genuine forecasting or investment value. Using a daily dataset of 3,823 observations spanning 18 October 2010 to 31 December 2025, sixteen standardized market, volatility, and macro-financial features are reduced via Principal Component Analysis (eight components explaining 92.1% of variance) and partitioned using K-Means clustering, validated against a Gaussian Mixture Model. The optimal solution, selected by silhouette score, identifies two statistically and economically distinct regimes, subsequently labelled Bull / Low-Risk (n = 3,201; 83.7% of observations) and Bear / High-Risk (n = 622; 16.3%). why: Standard regime detection; expected two-regime Bull/Bear finding.

title: The Experience Paradox Task Automation, Hiring Automation, and the Market That Stopped Evaluating
abstract: Three prominent 2026 studies of artificial intelligence and employment appear contradictory: (1) occupation-level employment declines among young workers in AI-exposed occupations, (2) firm level hiring increases among heavy AI adopters, and the (3) attribution of rising graduate unemployment to remote work. They also share a limitation, for each measure only the extensive margin of employment. None asks whether the work that survives still builds, or still rewards, accumulated judgment. This paper develops a two-axis framework distinguishing execution (codified task performance, subject to physical or algorithmic ceilings) from judgment (consequence-bearing discretion, which compounds with experience), and separates two conditions that current data cannot tell apart: (1) the destruction of experience's value and (2) the failure of the market that prices it. Evidence that generative AI transmits the practices of experienced workers to novices implies that the transmissible component of experience is depreciating; the consequence-bearing component is not, and its complement is expanding. Drawing on the litigation record of Mobley v. Workday, which makes the algorithmic screening layer observable at unprecedented scale although no finding on the merits has been made, we identify a paradox: task automation is raising the relative value of consequence-bearing judgment at precisely the moment hiring automation is reducing the probability that judgment is ever evaluated. The two failures compound across generations: with the formation of judgment disrupted among the young and its evaluation gated for the experienced, the judgment supply chain is severed at both ends, and an economy can run short of experience while excluding the people who have it. Rational adaptations to this collision, signal degradation and reversion to patronage channels, carry costs of their own. We close with five testable propositions and a measurement agenda for the experience margin.
why: Framework distinguishing execution from judgment; no empirics.

title: A Multi-Source Sustainability Intelligence System (MS-SIS) for Explainable Greenwashing Detection: A Design Science Approach Integrating ESG, Blockchain, and Geospatial Evidence
abstract: Greenwashing has become a critical challenge due to increasing reliance on Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) disclosures that are difficult to verify independently. Existing Sustainability Information Systems (SIS) often rely on individual data sources, limiting their ability to validate sustainability claims against objective evidence. Addressing this challenge from a Design Science Research (DSR) perspective, this study designs, develops, and evaluates a Multi-Source Sustainability Intelligence System (MS-SIS) that integrates ESG disclosures, blockchain-based carbon credit transactions, and satellite-derived geospatial observations. The proposed artifact incorporates a layered architecture comprising multi-source data integration, feature fusion, anomaly-aware analytics, predictive machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence (SHAP and LIME), and decision-support functionalities for greenwashing detection. The artifact was evaluated using an MS-SDGA-generated multi-source sustainability benchmark dataset through comparative experiments involving six supervised machine learning algorithms and three anomaly detection techniques. The results demonstrate the potential of integrating heterogeneous sustainability evidence for greenwashing detection, with XGBoost achieving the highest predictive performance of 95% accuracy and 0.98 ROC-AUC. The explainability component provides complementary global and local interpretations of model predictions, supporting transparent sustainability assessment. Beyond predictive performance, this research contributes to the Green IS and Information Systems literature by introducing a reusable sustainability intelligence artifact and design principles for developing transparent, explainable, and evidence-driven Sustainability Information Systems. The findings demonstrate how multi-source information integration can reduce information fragmentation and information asymmetry while providing decision-support capabilities for sustainability assessment and governance.
why: Greenwashing detection framework; deployment unclear.

title: A hybrid GARCH-LSTM model for Chinese carbon market volatility forecasting
abstract: Accurate forecasting of carbon market price volatility is of significant importance. The Chinese carbon market primarily relies on daily data, characterized by short time series and discontinuous trading, posing substantial challenges for volatility prediction. Constructing an integrated model that combines econometric models with deep learning is crucial for addressing the issues of long memory and structural breakpoints in carbon financial markets. This paper develops a comprehensive hybrid forecasting model that integrates the Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) family models with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) artificial neural networks, consisting of three stages. In the first stage, based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), all historical information up to time t is selected to estimate the benchmark GARCH model in a rolling-window fashion. In the second stage, the updated conditional volatility and standardized return series are used to construct a feature matrix incorporating multi-source information. In the third stage, this feature matrix is input into a pre-trained and fixed-parameter LSTM model to obtain the volatility forecast for time t+1. The empirical results demonstrate that compared to traditional GARCH volatility forecasting models, the prediction accuracy of the proposed method is significantly improved.
why: Chinese carbon market volatility; single market, standard approach.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Human Capital, and the Emergence of New Ventures
abstract: What happens to AI experts who leave academic roles to create their own AI companies? This paper examines the phenomenon using an empirical panel-data method. To determine the fate of artificial intelligence (AI) experts who leave academic positions to found their own AI businesses, it examines data from 2004 to 2018 from both institutions and startups. We want to know whether AI worker mobility impacts AI company development and funding opportunities; therefore, we're doing this research to find out. Examining if these impacts vary with tenure status, institution quality, and professors' deep learning competence is another focus of the research. To do this study, we will examine several conceptualizations of city characteristics and institutions. The study's conclusions were based on a wide range of opinions about institutional and municipal characteristics. The results show that several highly qualified AI educators left their positions over the research period. When many educators leave a school, few students stay, and those who remain often see a significant decrease in funding for artificial intelligence-based startups. After academics use deep learning, get tenure, or work at prestigious institutions, the negative effects are plain to discern. It is very unlikely that shocks at a level greater than the university or the municipality are responsible for the observed connections, according to several robustness tests. Students don't have enough practical experience with AI in the classroom, according to the research, which is a major factor in these outcomes. Students are finding it more difficult to establish enterprises, and entrepreneurs are finding it tougher to secure funding due to these barriers. The findings highlight the need to facilitate collaboration between companies and academic institutions and to retain AI experts on staff. Researchers hope that lawmakers and universities will use the study's findings to propose legislation that encourages educators to remain in the field as they gain expertise in artificial intelligence and startup companies.
why: AI expert mobility and startups; limited pre-modern AI sample.

title: Predictive Financial Analytics for Proactive Risk Management: A Quantitative Study of Volatility Forecasting in Indian Capital Markets
abstract: In recent years, the Indian capital markets have witnessed a remarkable development that has put them among the most sought-after investment places not only for the domestic but also for the international investor. The Nifty 50 index's 13.3% increase in 2024 alone can be attributed to the solid economic fundamentals and rising capital expenditures. However, this rapid growth has also led to greater market fluctuations that render accurate prediction and risk management even more important than before. Volatility, which denotes the degree to which asset prices vary, is a critical factor that affects investment strategies, portfolio performance and even policy-making. Among the various models, GARCH, a traditional one, has been most common in the estimation of volatility, but at the same time, it has been successful to a limited extent in capturing the non-linear aspects and sudden shifts in the forex market. On the other hand, the upswing of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods, particularly the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and the hybrid RNN-LSTM models, is offering a strong competitor by modeling the complex interdependence of the financial data accurately. This research project is about the use of AI-based predictive analytics to forecast market volatility in the Indian context. It involves a comparison of the traditional GARCH model with those based on LSTM and hybrid RNN-LSTM for the purpose of predicting market volatility using data from the Nifty 50 index's daily returns for the years 2015 to 2024. The standard evaluation metrics—MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and R²—along with the Diebold-Mariano test, are employed for determining model accuracy and statistical significance. The first model, LSTM, achieved a lower MAE (0.001), reduced RMSE (0.002), and a higher R² (0.92) compared to GARCH (MAE = 0.002, RMSE = 0.003, R² = 0.85). Besides, GARCH presents a baseline for volatility estimates. The machine learning models, as per the Diebold-Mariano test (p = 0.03), are significantly better than GARCH in forecasting accuracy. The research concludes that LSTM and hybrid RNN-LSTM architectures are on the top in AI-powered models and are the best for volatility forecasting and proactive risk management in Indian capital markets. Incorporation of macroeconomic indicators, high-frequency data, or sentiment analysis can be taken up in future research for better predictions and wider applicability of the model to other emerging markets.
why: Single-country volatility forecast; incomplete abstract, no out-of-sample evidence.

title: Ensemble Machine Learning Approach for Stock Market Classification: Predicting Performance Categories and Financial Risk Using Hybrid Models
abstract: The computational complexity of predicting the behavior of stock markets continues to be one of the most analytically intractable problems in quantitative finance, despite the nonlinearity, high dimension, and time volatility, which are inherent to the modern financial system. Although single machine learning models have shown encouraging performance in financial classification problems, all of them are prone to overfitting, instability in variance, and feature noise sensitivity, making them unsuitable to apply in the real world. The proposed and assessed hybrid ensemble machine learning structure is aimed at meeting the two tasks of the stock performance category prediction and financial risk classification. The presented architecture combines several heterogeneous base classifiers such as Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM with a stacked meta-learn architecture enhanced by sophisticated feature engineering using historical price changes, volume statistics, and technical indicators and basic financial ratios. A curated dataset of 4,000 equity records in various market sectors was experimented with and the performance was measured on a stratified held-out test set where the evaluation metrics were Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score and AUC-ROC. The proposed Hybrid Ensemble model achieved a classification accuracy of 92.1% and an AUC-ROC of 0.967, which outperformed all baseline models, including standalone gradient boosting and bagging. On financial risk classification into three tiers of risk (Low), (Moderate), (High), the model achieved macro-average F1-score of 0.918, which supports the equal and consistent performance of the model when exposed to a condition of class imbalance. The analysis of the importance of features demonstrated that Price-to-Earnings ratio, RSI, and MACD Signal Divergence are the most significant predictors, which proves the value of combining fundamental and technical spheres of features. The results of these experiments are strong empirical evidence of the advantage of hybrid ensemble structures in the financial classification task and the potential of their implementation in the portfolio management and algorithmic risk evaluation systems.
why: Generic ensemble, no out-of-sample discipline shown.

title: Beyond AI Hype | Introducing the Clinical Alpha Framework for Healthcare Equity Valuation
abstract: Artificial intelligence has become one of the most influential investment themes in healthcare. Yet much of the current discussion continues to treat AI exposure as a sufficient proxy for future value creation. This perspective article introduces the Clinical Alpha Framework, a new conceptual model proposed by the author to distinguish between two mechanisms of value creation in AI-enabled healthcare companies: AI Alpha and Clinical Alpha. AI Alpha represents value generated by technological narratives, investor expectations, and perceived innovation potential. Clinical Alpha represents value generated through verifiable clinical evidence, regulatory validation, real-world adoption, and measurable improvements in healthcare delivery and patient outcomes. To formalize this distinction, the article introduces three original conceptual tools: the Clinical Alpha Matrix, a two-dimensional classification framework; the Proposed Clinical Alpha Index (PCAI), a theoretical scoring model for assessing clinical value creation; and AI-Clinical Divergence (ACD), which captures the degree of misalignment between market enthusiasm and validated clinical performance. The central proposition is that while AI Alpha may dominate valuation dynamics in the short term, Clinical Alpha is more likely to determine sustainable value creation over longer investment horizons.
why: Conceptual framework; AI Alpha vs Clinical Alpha framing.

title: Machine Learning versus Deep Learning for Public Financial Report Classification and Popularity Prediction: A Feasibility Study on Ghana's Controller and Accountant-general's Department
abstract: Government agencies increasingly publish financial reports online, but small public-sector portals rarely have the labeled data needed to test automated classification tools. This study evaluates the feasibility of these tools using a corpus of 131 official reports from Ghana's Controller and Accountant-General's Department (CAGD). We compare classical machine learning models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting [XGBoost] with Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique [SMOTE]) and character-level deep learning models (bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory [LSTM] and Text Convolutional Neural Network [TextCNN]) across three tasks: category prediction, binary popularity classification, and log-download forecasting. Models were evaluated using a stratified 70/15/15 train, validation, and test split, randomized hyperparameter search, and a final finetuning phase. The fine-tuned XGBoost classifier achieved 1.00 accuracy on the five-class category task. Logistic Regression reached 0.75 accuracy (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve [ROC-AUC] of 0.80) on the binary popularity task, and Random Forest reached an R-squared of 0.85 on log downloads. An ablation study removing twenty-five keyword features dropped category accuracy from 1.00 to 0.80, a stable drop across five randomized data splits. This indicates keyword features inflated initial results, though remaining performance confirms the models learn nontautological structure. This work serves as an honest feasibility check, showing that thorough feature ablation is essential before deploying these models on live government portals.
why: Feasibility study, 131 reports; sample too small.

title: Exchange Rate Volatility Spillovers to Gold Prices in Sri Lanka: Evidence from a Hybrid Econometric-Machine Learning Framework
abstract: This study examines spillovers of means and volatilities between the exchange rates and the gold price in Sri Lanka. Both linear and nonlinear spillover channels are explored under a hybrid econometric-machine learning framework. The data consists of daily spot price of local gold and USD/LKR exchange rate over the period 2018-2025. In terms of methodology, the empirical strategy includes Granger causality test, HAC regression of volatility, various GARCH models, Random Forest estimator, and time series cross-validation. It was found that exchange rates strongly influence gold prices and provide predictive signals for future movements. The volatility regression revealed a positive relationship between the exchangerate volatility and the gold-market volatility. Nonetheless, the GARCH model showed that the relationship is not significant in dynamic and conditional settings, even after controlling for volatility persistence, suggesting little evidence of structural volatility transmission. Volatility persistence in the Sri Lankan gold market is quite high (α + β = 0.947). Random Forest estimator has a very good fit, explaining 95.89% of variation in volatility of gold market. Lagged gold and exchange-rate volatility proved the most informative predictors in the regression. The forecasting model was validated using time-series cross-validation. This study emphasises the importance of distinguishing between structural spillover channel and predictability of financial markets in risk transmission process. The study provides original evidence based on combining econometric and machine learning methods in an emerging economy.
why: Single-country exchange-rate correlation; limited scope, not transferable.

title: WHEN YIELD ISN'T RETURN: USD/INR, Foreign-Investor G-Secs, AI Capital Reallocation and the 2026 Rupee Pressure
abstract: This research note examines the 2026 depreciation of the Indian rupee against the U.S. dollar despite India's strong external buffers and a positive India–U.S. 10-year yield differential. It analyses the interaction of oil prices, foreign portfolio flows, global dollar conditions, fiscal composition, RBI intervention and the emerging global AI investment cycle. A central investment question is whether India's higher sovereign bond yield translates into superior returns for foreign investors once INR depreciation and duration risk are considered. Using the 18 August 2026 market levels, the note estimates a carry-only one-year FX break-even of approximately ₹97.62/$ for an Indian 10-year yield of 6.827% versus a U.S. 10-year yield of 4.708%. The analysis also examines India's foreign-investor G-Sec policy reforms, including tax and market-access changes, and contrasts FY26 FPI equity outflows with continued debt inflows. It proposes AI-related capital allocation as a testable additional channel for explaining international portfolio reallocation, while explicitly avoiding a causal conclusion because the destination of Indian equity outflows is not directly observed. The note concludes that the 2026 episode represents market pressure within a substantially stronger external balance sheet than in 1991, rather than a classical external-financing crisis. It identifies several empirical avenues for further research, including econometric analysis of oil, FPI flows, RBI intervention and AI-related investment.
why: USD/INR analysis specific to 2026; market commentary not methods.

title: Bank Regulatory Instruments and Financial Stability in the Artificial Intelligence Era: Application of the Random-Effects Generalized Least Squares (RE-GLS) and System GMM
abstract: This paper investigates how the capital adequacy ratio and the liquid asset ratio affect the stability of banks, which is measured by the Z-score of Turkish commercial banks addressing a notable gap in the empirical literature on bank regulation and stability within the Turkish context. Using a balanced panel of 14 BDDK-licensed commercial banks observed quarterly over 2016: Q1–2025: Q4, the study employs random-effects GLS, Difference GMM, and two-step System GMM estimators to regress the Z-score on the three regulatory variables. The empirical findings consistently confirm that LATA, CAR, and ETA each exert a statistically significant positive effect on bank stability across all specifications (p
why: 14 Turkish banks only; single country with limited scope.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning and Causal Discovery for Accounting Policy Change: An Explainable Dynamic Impact Assessment Framework
abstract: The efficiency and profitability of a company are significantly impacted whenever there is a change in accounting technique. The complex causal links and lag effects make it difficult to determine the consequences with certainty. Our proposed approach, DQN-CD4APC, which stands for "Deep Q Network-based Causal Discovery for Accounting Policy Change," is a means to investigate the long-term effects of accounting policy changes. This research employs a dynamic Bayesian network, a deep Q-network (DQN), a better PC algorithm, a knowledge graph for accounting, and a better PC algorithm to determine the effects and causes of regulations on Shanghai and Shenzhen enterprises. To begin, the superior PC approach uses the accounting knowledge tree to build a multidimensional feature space that will serve as a foundation for future work. Second, with the support of a payment system, DQN may judiciously research and improve causal discovery pathways, enabling it to discover key causal linkages. Lastly, a dynamic Bayesian network has emerged, allowing for multi-step policy impact computation. Compared to more conventional approaches, DQN-CD4APC performs much better in studies when it comes to determining the causal structure. Accelerating the model's convergence, predicting policy effects with an accuracy of 89.6 percent, and increasing the F1 value by 18.7 percent are all benefits. Accounting rule changes, inaccurate accounting data, and weak business risk management may all be easily monitored with the help of the proposed framework, according to the findings. From a policymaking perspective, the framework may aid business and government authorities in understanding the implications of future laws, as well as in developing more effective methods to regulate accounting and manage risk.
why: Complex accounting policy DRL paper; vague abstract, no validation.

title: A deep learning-driven iterative scheme for high-dimensional HJB equations in portfolio selection with price impact
abstract: In this paper, we conduct a study of the portfolio selection problem, incorporating both exogenous (proportional) and endogenous (resulting from liquidity risk, characterized by a stochastic process) transaction costs through the utility-based approach. We also consider the intrinsic relationship between these two types of costs. To address the associated nonlinear two-dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, we propose an innovative deep learning-driven policy iteration scheme with three key advantages: i) it has the potential to address the curse of dimensionality; ii) it is adaptable to problems involving high-dimensional control spaces; iii) it eliminates truncation errors. The numerical analysis of the proposed scheme, including convergence analysis in a general setting, is also discussed. To illustrate the impact of these two types of transaction costs on portfolio choice, we conduct through numerical experiments using three typical utility functions.
why: Deep learning for HJB equations; pure theory, no empirical validation.

title: The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Brand Equity: A Comparative Analysis of Human-AI Participation Ratios and Digital Touchpoints.
abstract: Is AI-generated content quietly eroding brand equity? Generative AI is being adopted across brand touchpoints above all to cut costs, yet it remains unclear whether those savings come at the expense of the brand itself. This study argues that the answer is not uniform: it hinges on context, and specifically on the sector and the touchpoint where AI is deployed. The question is pressing precisely now, as AI-generated content grows increasingly indistinguishable from human-authored content and as new transparency rules (such as the EU AI Act's disclosure obligations for synthetic and deepfake content) make the labelling of AI involvement unavoidable. The work therefore speaks to a live commercial and regulatory reality, not to theory alone. To test where human participation still earns its cost, the study pairs a netnographic analysis of customer reviews across the four quadrants of the Foote-Cone-Belding grid with two controlled experiments set in email and social media touchpoints. The results reveal a two-regime logic: in communication, what matters is consumers' involvement with the product rather than whether the category is rational or emotional; in service recovery, human presence becomes decisive. A non-monotonic "hybrid valley" also surfaces, in which evenly balanced human-AI content can underperform both clearly human and clearly AI-led alternatives. One tension stands out. When asked outright, consumers voice a clear preference for human-made communication; yet how they actually judge the content departs from that stated preference, even when the AI's role is fully disclosed. The study offers marketers a touchpoint-by-touchpoint framework for calibrating human-AI collaboration, and fresh evidence on the limits of authenticity as the mechanism behind AI's impact on brands. AI disclosure: generative AI tools were used to support language editing; all research design, data collection, analysis, and interpretation were carried out by the author.
why: Marketing study on AI brand erosion.

title: Q-ALU: Quant Asymmetric Leaky Unit: A Market Psychology Aware Activation Function with Downside Risk Protection for High Frequency Quantitative Trading and Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Deep neural networks applied to high frequency trading (HFT) and algorithmic portfolio management frequently suffer from structural inductive mismatch. Prevailing activation functions, including the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU), Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU), and Swish/SiLU, were fundamentally designed for computer vision and natural language processing under the implicit assumption of isotropic, symmetric feature representations. Financial price discovery, however, is inherently asymmetric: downside liquidations and panic cascades occur with substantially greater velocity and severity than bullish accumulation phases, as formalized by Kahneman and Tversky prospect theory. Furthermore, intermediate hidden representations in trading models are severely corrupted by microstructure noise (for example bid ask bounce), leading to rampant overtrading and catastrophic policy collapse in reinforcement learning algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). To resolve these challenges, this paper introduces the Quant Asymmetric Leaky Unit (Q-ALU), a novel activation function custom engineered for financial time series modeling and deep reinforcement learning. Q-ALU couples a dynamic hyperbolic tangent momentum riding regime on the positive domain with an exponential to linear downside barrier on the negative domain. We mathematically prove that Q-ALU is globally monotonic (f ′ (x) ≥ 0 ∀x ∈ R), possesses a C 0 continuous origin, and exhibits a novel Dynamic Gradient Overshoot, delivering a +13.53% sensitivity spike at the critical drawdown threshold x =-2δ before relaxing into linear cut loss tracking. In empirical evaluations on 5,000 out of sample ticks (from a 10,000 tick multi regime stream) under realistic transaction costs (1.0 to 1.5 bps fee per turnover), neural trading policies equipped with Q-ALU achieve an out of sample return of +75.85% with a Per-Step Sortino of 0.142, a Profit Factor of 2.09, and a Maximum Drawdown (MDD) of 2.79%, vastly outperforming baseline architectures utilizing ReLU (+5.43% return, 0.95% MDD) and GELU (+1.42% return, 0.01% MDD). Furthermore, when evaluated across 2,834 real world high frequency market bars of BTC/USDT and implemented within Temporal 1D Convolutional Neural Networks across 5 random seeds, Q-ALU demonstrates consistent alpha generation and superior fee resistance. Finally, we provide numerically stable, production grade PyTorch modules and hardware optimized CUDA C++ kernels achieving up to 133 million evaluations per second.
why: Novel activation function for HFT; no empirical validation.

title: Digital Image Classification Forecasting of Technical Stock Price Patterns
abstract: We categorize stock price patterns by their five consecutive extrema following rules outlined in literature. We smooth stock prices in a fixed window and locate extrema from the maxima and minima in the smooth prices. We then plot a digital image using 200 pixel values of each pattern and turn the image into grey scale and then black and white to locate the pixel values. We determine each unique pixel value representing the extrema. We repeat the process to determine that the pixel no values categorize the patterns the same as the price time series. Then we train a machine learning classifier on each labeled pattern example represented by their consecutive extrema. We find a high degree of accuracy on both in sample and out of sample classification data. The method chosen is gradient boosted trees. We then remove the extrema one at a time and re classify using approximately 50% of the data for training on all five extrema and 50% for testing on removed extrema. We see that misclassification occurs between top and bottom patterns. We then re train our classifier using 10% of the data and categorize all of our top patterns as 'top' and bottom as 'bot. Key Takeaways: 1. Digital image processing and machine learning can be used for early detection of technical stock price patterns prior to their completion. 2. Misclassification occurs between top class and bottom class patterns (i.e. a Rectangle Top is Classified as a Head and Shoulders) 3. Patterns categorized by 'top' or 'bottom' are better than 98% accurate for forecasting on pixel values representing their extrema compared to around 50% for time series observations so image processing is a better method for detecting and forecasting patterns via Machine Learning as opposed to using raw time series.
why: Gimmicky image encoding; no rigorous cost analysis

title: Predicting Corporate Green Innovation using ESG Indicators: The Approach of Deep Learning Models
abstract: Green innovation has become increasingly important for reducing the environmental impacts of corporate activities and supporting sustainable development. Drawing on the Resource-Based View (RBV), this study examines the predictive role of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) indicators, financial characteristics, and firm-specific attributes in corporate green innovation. The study contributes to the literature by applying deep learning models, particularly Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, to predict firm-level green innovation and by comparing their predictive performance with a conventional Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) benchmark. Using data from Chinese A-listed firms from 2018 to 2022, the study integrates financial and non-financial indicators within a comprehensive predictive framework. The results demonstrate that ESG indicators provide important information for predicting corporate green innovation and that the ANN and LSTM models outperform the conventional OLS benchmark in predictive performance. Among the evaluated models, ANN achieves the highest predictive accuracy. These findings demonstrate the potential of deep learning approaches for capturing complex patterns in corporate sustainability data and provide useful implications for managers, investors, and policymakers seeking to promote green innovation and sustainable corporate development.
why: Green innovation ESG prediction; standard ML, single country.

title: Agentic AI and Airline Pricing: Demand Cliffs, Elasticity Migration, and the Fate of Fare Fencing under Delegated Booking
abstract: Autonomous AI agents that search, compare, and book flights on travelers' behalf are moving from demonstration to deployment, while airline pricing theory largely presumes a human buyer. This paper develops a formal framework for airline markets in which the buyer is an algorithm. A traveler's booking instruction is modeled as a machine-readable delegation contract, comprising a budget cap, a departure window, a preferred carrier with a switching threshold, and a patience budget, executed by the agent as a deterministic threshold policy. A population of contracts then induces a demand function equal to the survival function of the budget-cap distribution, a step-like schedule that inherits the atoms of the cap distribution as demand cliffs and renders drip pricing allocatively inert. Deterministic simulation experiments trace the consequences through a mixed human, agent market as agent penetration rises. Price sensitivity migrates from the whole fare range to a small set of contract thresholds, a shift summarized by an elasticity concentration index. The optimal posted fare comes to shadow the cap atoms, reaching them through a discrete jump or a gradual creep depending on their position relative to the human optimum, and remaining pinned thereafter. Maximized profit rises with penetration when stated caps track valuations and falls when caps sit below them. Intertemporal fare fencing loses its premium as delegation severs the correlation between purchase timing and valuation, surviving only where the joint distribution of contract parameters reconstructs it. Implications for revenue management, loyalty programs, and distribution strategy are discussed.
why: Airline pricing with agents; formal theory only, no empirical test.

title: Governing Artificial Intelligence as an ESG Issue
abstract: Purpose-Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly operates both as an ESG-enabling capability and as an ESG exposure in its own right. This article examines how corporate AI affects sustainability measurement, environmental performance, workforce outcomes, information governance, internal controls, board accountability and disclosure credibility. Design/ methodology/approach: The study employs a structured integrative evidence synthesis. It consolidates the evidence base in the author's 2026 working paper. It updates it through targeted validation of recent peer-reviewed empirical studies, systematic and bibliometric reviews, and official sources from the International Energy Agency, United Nations Environment Programme, World Economic Forum, NIST, OECD, IFRS Foundation, Securities and Exchange Board of India and European Union. Evidence is coded across six domains: ESG measurement and reporting, environmental footprint, social and workforce impact, governance and model risk, supply-chain due diligence, and regulatory/assurance implications. Findings-The literature supports a conditional dual effect. AI can improve ESG data extraction, green innovation, information governance, anomaly detection, climate risk analysis, and internal control quality. Yet the same systems can generate material environmental and governance liabilities through electricity and water demand, opaque or biased models, hallucination, cybersecurity and privacy exposure, vendor dependence, workforce disruption and uncertain responsibility. The most important unresolved issue is therefore not whether AI can support ESG, but whether firms can produce an auditable chain of evidence demonstrating that AI-supported ESG decisions and disclosures are reliable, lawful and accountable. Originality/value-The article develops an eight-gate AI-ESG Accountability Cycle and a claimlevel assurance chain linking materiality, data provenance, model validation, human authority, environmental footprint, social impact, disclosure evidence and board oversight. It also maps the framework to BRSR/BRSR Core, IFRS S1/S2,
why: Integrative review of AI as ESG issue.

title: Digital Transformation Capabilities and Supply Chain Finance Resilience: An Integrated AI-Blockchain-analytics Framework
abstract: Supply chain finance (SCF) plays a pivotal role in maintaining liquidity and operational continuity across global value networks. However, systemic supply chain disruptions, macroeconomic volatility, and information asymmetry frequently expose SCF programs to severe friction and default risks. While digital transformation is widely touted as a catalyst for supply chain resilience, empirical evidence regarding the explicit mechanisms through which distinct digital transformation capabilities enhance Supply Chain Finance Resilience (SCFR) remains fragmented. Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV), Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), and Information Processing Theory (IPT), this study develops and tests an integrated framework evaluating the direct and indirect impacts of Artificial Intelligence Capability (AIC), Blockchain Capability (BC), and Data Analytics Capability (DAC) on SCFR, mediated by Digital Trust in SCF Platforms (DT). Using a computational research simulation methodology, a respondent-level dataset (𝑁 = 500) representing supply chain, finance, operations, and IT decision-makers across international enterprises was algorithmically generated under a defensible latent-variable covariance structure. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was executed to evaluate the measurement and structural models. The structural analysis reveals that AIC (𝛽 = 0.241, 𝑝 This methodological prototype advances theoretical understanding by unpacking the granular capability configurations necessary to foster digital trust and financial resilience in supply networks. For practitioners and policymakers, the findings highlight that investing in blockchain technology yields minimal resilience benefits unless coupled with platform-wide digital trust mechanisms, whereas AI and analytics offer dual-pathway benefits across operational and relational domains.
why: Survey-based supply chain finance framework.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Stock Market Prediction Using Technical Indicators: A Variational Quantum Neural Network Approach
abstract: This paper presents a novel Variational Quantum Neural Network (VQNN) framework for stock market directional prediction by encoding classical technical indicators Relative Strength Index (RSI), Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD), and Signal Line directly into quantum circuit amplitudes via RY rotation gates. A 5-qubit parameterized circuit employing Hadamard superposition, entangling CNOT layers, and variational RZ rotations is trained using gradient-based parameter-shift rules on simulated S&P 500 daily data spanning 2,000 trading sessions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed VQNN achieves 85.4% directional accuracy and an F1-score of 0.841, outperforming classical baselines including SVM (72.3%), LSTM (74.8%), CNN (73.1%), and hybrid quantum-SVM (79.6%). The circuit operates in a 2⁵ = 32-dimensional Hilbert space while requiring only three encoding parameters, exhibiting exponential feature-space expressibility relative to classical linear kernel methods. Bloch sphere analysis reveals that the RY encoding faithfully preserves the semantic ordering of RSI market states (oversold/neutral/overbought). These findings suggest achievable quantum advantage in financial time-series classification within the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) device era.
why: Toy benchmark; 85% accuracy on technical indicators is overfitting.

title: Extended Controllability and AI-Driven Financial Reporting: Rethinking Revenue Recognition and Credit Risk under IFRS 9 and IFRS 15
abstract: Purpose: This paper proposes an "extended controllability" framework-defined as the alignment between accounting principles and the feasible scope of operational controls, which AI expands from discrete points to continuous transaction lifecycles-to revisit revenue recognition and credit risk practices under IFRS 9 and IFRS 15 (IASB, 2014a; IASB, 2014b). It demonstrates that certain long-standing accounting constraints are not inherent but arise from a historical gap between the intended scope of principles and the feasible scope of controls. Design/methodology/approach: Drawing on conceptual analysis and the literature on continuous auditing and institutional theory (Power, 1997; Power, 2010), an analytical framework is developed to distinguish inherent constraints from historical-technological ones. Two proofs of concept-"individual customer credit assessment" and a "stepwise profit adjustment model for contracts"-are designed to show how AI can turn previously rigid dilemmas into designable choices (Dai and Vasarhelyi, 2017; Kokina and Davenport, 2017). Findings: The hybrid individual-assessment model can simultaneously satisfy the matching and prudence principles and offers an alternative to collective provisioning under IFRS 9 (Novotny-Farkas, 2016). The stepwise profit adjustment model bridges the gap between the traditional method (point-in-time revenue recognition at delivery) and the percentage-of-completion method (confined to continuous transfer of control), recognising profit in line with actual progress of productive activity (Wüstemann and Wüstemann, 2020). Both models maintain institutional reliability, conditional upon establishing an algorithmic governance framework (including explainability and management-resistant design) (No and Vasarhelyi, 2022; Munoko et al., 2020). Limitations and practical implications: The paper is a conceptual-theoretical analysis; empirical testing requires future research (Ball, 2016; Schipper, 2010). Nevertheless, the proposed framework carries direct implications for standard-setters. By discussing the risks of an "algorithmic panopticon" and the necessity of explainability, the paper also examines the socio-institutional implications of transitioning to these models (Zuboff, 2019). Originality/value: By integrating professional experience with theoretical analysis, the paper moves beyond critique and offers a "critical-constructive" framework for standard-setting in the digital age. The ontological separation of inherent and historical-technological constraints, and the conceptualisation of an "inception margin", equip the accounting literature with an analytical tool for assessing the technological maturity of reporting practices (Chambers, 1966; Sterling, 1970).
why: Position paper on accounting standards, not financial ML.

title: Artificial Intelligence, China, U.S. Fiscal Imbalances, Dollar Primacy, and the Outlook for Inflation, Recession, and Bank Valuation An Integrated Macroeconomic and Banking-Sector Scenario Analysis Revised August 22, 2026
abstract: This paper develops an integrated three-year framework for evaluating U.S. inflation, recession risk, and bank profitability and valuation in the presence of interacting forces: rapid artificial-intelligence investment and prospective productivity gains; China's structural economic slowdown and demographic aging; geopolitical risk centered on Taiwan; persistent U.S. federal deficits and rising public debt; uncertainty over the long-run international role of the U.S. dollar; and, in this revised version, the 2026 Iran-Hormuz conflict and prediction-market evidence. The central conclusion is asymmetric. AI productivity and Chinese disinflation can support a favorable soft-landing regime in which inflation declines while real growth remains positive. Persistent fiscal deficits and energy/geopolitical risk, however, may keep long-term Treasury yields and equity discount rates higher than would otherwise be expected. The Hormuz episode adds a meaningful probability of a high-rate, slow-growth regime even if it does not by itself cause recession. Prediction markets continue to place low single-digit to low-teens probabilities on near-term China-Taiwan military outcomes, but the conditional macroeconomic loss from a Taiwan blockade or invasion remains extreme. For banks, deposit-franchise quality, liquidity, profitability, credit quality, securities duration, and capital strength remain especially important determinants of relative valuation.
why: Macro scenario analysis; position paper, not replicable method.

title: Becoming an AI-Native Bank: A Practitioner Framework for the Operating Layer
abstract: Incumbent banks have invested in artificial intelligence while leaving much of the work that agents must perform embedded in fragmented data, documents, informal judgement and disconnected controls. This practitioner position paper calls the institutional foundation that makes such work executable the operating layer. It defines an AI-native bank as an organisation in which an authorised agent can act on verified business facts, codified policy, controlled workflows and callable capabilities. Each action must also be evaluated, attributable and open to human intervention. The argument combines the 2026 move towards enterprise deployment vehicles, public evidence on AI returns, established risk standards and professional observation in financial-services architecture. It applies the theory of constraints to distinguish model adoption from business value, then develops a working framework for operating-layer readiness. The framework links seven architectural properties to four phases of delivery: diagnostic, codification, build and bound, and handover. Regulatory binding and executive translation are integrated into that delivery discipline. The central claim is that codification creates a reusable institutional asset. AI can reduce the cost of producing the asset, while human owners preserve warrant through approval, versioning, audit and change control. Testable propositions define an agenda for future case research. The framework is conceptual and practice-informed; causal effects across banks remain to be tested.
why: Practitioner position paper; architectural framework, no implementation.

title: Predicting Recovery in Group Long-Term Disability Insurance with Optimized Explainable Machine Learning
abstract: We study prediction of compiled recovery values for non-maternity Group Long-Term Disability claims. Using the predictor set of Kopinsky (2018), we add interpretable engineered features for categorical variables and duration, fit CatBoost, XGBoost, and multilayer perceptron models, and tune hyperparameters with Optuna. We evaluate the models on a held-out test set and use SHAP to summarize global feature importance and claimant-level prediction decompositions. CatBoost and XGBoost obtain the lowest errors and substantially improve on the decisiontree benchmark. Across models, benefit amount, disability category, duration, and age are the main predictors of fitted recovery values. The results show that machine-learning methods can improve GLTD recovery prediction while retaining interpretability.
why: Long-term disability claims; insurance not financial markets.

title: Design Principles for AI Auditing Systems in Credit Scoring Under the EU AI Act: A Design Science Literature Review
abstract: Credit scoring systems built on machine learning are classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act (Regulation EU 2024/1689), triggering binding obligations spanning risk management, data governance, transparency, human oversight, and robustness. While a growing body of research addresses individual components of AI auditing—bias detection, explainability, fairness metrics, compliance architecture—these strands remain fragmented and rarely map systematically onto the Act's specific legal provisions. This paper asks: what design principles should guide the development of AI auditing systems for credit scoring to ensure EU AI Act compliance? Using Design Science Research and a structured thematic review of a curated academic corpus, the study identifies five thematic clusters spanning regulatory traceability, multi-dimensional and automated auditing, fairness and subgroup accountability, explainability-fairness convergence, and architectural embedding of compliance. From these clusters, the paper derives eight Compliance-by-Design principles—covering regulatory traceability, lifecycle coverage, multi-dimensional assessment, automation, subgroup-aware fairness, bias documentation, dual-layer explainability, and compliance by architecture—that together constitute a Dynamic Compliance Architecture in which regulatory compliance is a native, continuous, and automated property of the auditing system rather than an ex-post overlay. The principles offer financial institutions a concrete design checklist ahead of the Act's August 2026 enforcement deadline, give RegTech vendors a basis for product differentiation, and provide regulators a structured lens for distinguishing substantive from cosmetic compliance. The study contributes nascent design theory at the intersection of AI governance, financial regulation, and information systems design.
why: Regulatory design principles; not methods paper.

title: Beyond the Textbook Consensus: Capital Budgeting Technique Choice (NPV, IRR, Payback) Across Institutional Regimes — A Comparative Synthesis and Atlas
abstract: Corporate finance textbooks converge on a single normative answer to the capital budgeting problem: firms should rank and accept projects using Net Present Value (NPV), because NPV alone correctly aggregates the time value of money and the magnitude of value created. Five decades of field surveys, beginning with Graham and Harvey's (2001) landmark study of U.S. Chief Financial Officers, show a persistently different empirical picture. Internal Rate of Return (IRR) and, in many countries, the simple Payback Period rule remain co-dominant or outright dominant decision criteria. This monograph does not run a new primary survey. Instead, it performs the synthesis that the dispersed country-level literature has not yet produced: it collects roughly thirty published field studies spanning North America, Western and Central-Eastern Europe, East Asia, South Asia, Oceania, Southern Africa and Latin America, organizes them into a common comparative skeleton, and asks a single organizing question-for which countries, and under which institutional conditions, was IRR, NPV, or Payback the more relevant criterion in practice? Building on this synthesis, the book proposes an original secondary artifact, the Institutional Capital Budgeting Index (ICBI), which scores each covered country-study on its distance from the textbook NPV consensus as a function of four recurring institutional correlates identified across the literature: capital market depth, legal origin and investor protection, average CFO financial education, and typical firm size/ownership concentration in the sampled population. The exercise is explicitly conceptual-synthetic: the ICBI is a transparent recombination of already-published percentages, not a new empirical estimate, and every score is traceable to a cited source. The clearest finding of the synthesis is not about any single country-it is about the map itself: capital budgeting technique choice has been surveyed intensively in the United States, Western Europe, Japan, Australia and, more recently, Central-Eastern Europe and parts of Asia, while Latin America has exactly one region-wide survey (Maquieira, Preve and Sarria-Allende, 2012, covering seven countries but explicitly excluding Brazil) plus a handful of single-country Brazilian studies, and large parts of Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East remain essentially unsurveyed. The book closes by arguing that this asymmetry, not any single technique-choice finding, is the most policy-relevant gap in the literature, and sets out a concrete research agenda for closing it. Use of Artificial Intelligence: this manuscript was produced with the assistance of a large language model (Claude, Anthropic) for literature synthesis support, drafting, and editorial structuring, under the direct supervision, verification, and final authorship responsibility of the named author. All cited findings were checked against the original published sources listed in the References section before inclusion. No primary data was collected, simulated, or fabricated for this work; the Institutional Capital Budgeting Index presented in Part III is explicitly and transparently a secondary recombination of previously published percentages, not new empirical evidence.
why: Capital budgeting monograph; survey/synthesis format.

title: Nonlinear Trade-Offs in Genai Application Pricing: A Game-Theoretic Analysis of API and Psychological Costs
abstract: In the rapidly evolving generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) ecosystem, downstream application providers face persistent challenges in designing optimal pricing strategies. These challenges arise from dual cost pressures: application programming interface (API) costs imposed by upstream model platforms and psychological frictions experienced by end consumers. This study develops a game-theoretic model to analyze application providers' strategic choice between subscriptionbased and usage-based pricing under both monopolistic and duopolistic market structures. The analysis reveals that the optimal strategies are shaped by a nonlinear interplay among psychological costs, model API costs, and consumer valuation. Under low psychological-cost conditions, API costs exert an inverted U-shaped effect on competing providers' profits. By contrast, under high API-cost regimes, subscription-based and usage-based models exhibit asymmetric sensitivities to psychological costs: profits under usage-based pricing decline with rising psychological costs, whereas subscription-based profits stabilise. Fthermore, elevated API and psychological costs attenuate competitive intensity, driving duopolistic equilibria toward monopoly-like outcomes. These findings remain robust after incorporating a broad set of realistic market frictions. The results provide actionable insights for GenAI application providers balancing cost pass-through, user engagement, and competitive positioning in pricing decisions.
why: GenAI pricing game theory; pure theory without empirical test.

title: The AI-EPS Dual Effect How Artificial Intelligence Regularly Adds to and Subtracts from Reported Earnings A Recurring Financial-reporting and Technology-renewal Framework
abstract: Artificial intelligence can affect earnings per share in opposite directions within the same reporting period and on a recurring basis. It may regularly add to earnings through revenue, productivity, capacity utilisation, error reduction and operating-cost efficiency. It may simultaneously and regularly subtract from earnings through service and operating expenditure; depreciation or amortisation of recognised AI resources; continuing implementation, training and governance costs; and the accelerated economic obsolescence, impairment or derecognition of existing technology. Conventional discussion often isolates one side of this continuing relationship. This conceptual and doctrinal paper proposes the Recurring AI-EPS Dual Effect: regular AI-related benefits and regular AI-related costs can coexist within the same reporting period and recur across successive periods. The construct is operationalised through a shareholder-facing disclosure taxonomy separating recurring operating benefits from recurring recognised costs, estimate changes and obsolescence charges, together with a four-gate Technology Vibrancy Cycle governing technology-renewal decisions. The additive/subtractive EPS identity is supporting notation rather than an independent analytical claim. The framework distinguishes accounting expense, taxable deduction, current tax, deferred tax and cash flow; it rejects any automatic claim that a book write-off generates a tax saving, finances replacement or is compensated by indirect taxes. It remains a testable conceptual model rather than an empirically proven causal relationship.
why: AI-EPS conceptual framework; position paper, no empirical work.

title: No Single Gate: Distributed AI Governance in Ghana's 2026 Financial-Sector Cyber Directive, and Implications for Digital Product Teams
abstract: In March 2026, the Bank of Ghana revised its Cyber and Information Security Directive (CISD) and built artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) governance obligations into at least six distinct locations across the document, rather than concentrating them in a single AIspecific clause: board-level AI literacy, contractual due diligence for AI and algorithmic service providers, a dedicated Digital Innovations part, a standalone part on cyber and information security requirements for AI systems, AI/ML-specific technical testing, and a dedicated annexure of AI/ML governance and control guidelines. This exceeds what the directive gives its other major cross-cutting priorities, including third-party risk, cloud computing, and access control. One month later, the United States' banking agencies revised their own foundational model risk guidance and explicitly excluded generative and agentic AI from its scope, deferring the question to future rulemaking (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System et al., 2026). This paper uses that contrast, and the wider literature on AI governance's uneasy inheritance from model risk management (Kurshan et al., 2020; Vukovic et al., 2025), to argue that CISD 2026's distributed design has a specific, underexamined consequence for Ghana's digital product organisations: a single AI governance owner or a late compliance sign-off cannot satisfy a framework built this way. The argument has sharpened further since the directive's release: in March 2026, MTN Ghana's mobile money business was structurally separated into a distinct, separately licensed entity, meaning product teams building on top of it must now coordinate across a genuine corporate boundary. A composite illustrative case shows what those costs when discovered late. The paper closes with a practical checklist and an agenda for empirical research.
why: Regulatory analysis of Ghana cyber directive.

title: Digital Payments vs. Microfinance: A Machine Learning and Econometric Evaluation of Financial Inclusion, Inequality, and Welfare Heterogeneity in Emerging Economies (2010–2023)
abstract: Financial inclusion remains one of the most consequential unsolved problems in global development economics, yet the causal mechanisms through which competing policy paradigms generate differential welfare outcomes across income distributions in emerging economies remain deeply contested. This paper addresses the fundamental empirical gap at the intersection of fintech, microfinance, and distributional economics through a rigorous, multi-method causal analysis synthesizing panel data from 47 developing economies spanning 2010 to 2023, yielding 611 countryyear observations. We construct two validated composite policy treatment variables: the Digital Payment Intensity Index (DPII, Cronbach alpha = 0.87), capturing mobile money penetration, digital transaction volumes, and real-time payment system maturity; and the Microfinance Intensity Index (MII, Cronbach alpha = 0.83), capturing MFI borrower penetration, gross loan portfolio depth, and deposit mobilization. Our causal identification deploys five complementary strategies: two-way fixed effects (TWFE) panel estimation with country and year fixed effects; heterogeneity-robust staggered Difference-in-Differences using the Callaway-Sant'Anna estimator; Instrumental Variables (2SLS) regression with mobile tower rollout and NGO density instruments; Double Machine Learning (DML) using Random Forest nuisance learners with five-fold cross-fitting; and Causal Forest estimation of Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). These strategies are complemented by XGBoost outcome modeling with SHAP feature attribution for characterizing nonlinear interaction structures. Results reveal that a one standard deviation increase in DPII is associated with a 6.8 to 8.3 percentage point gain in formal account ownership (p
why: Development economics not financial ML

title: The Windows XP Trap: How "Good Enough" Artificial Intelligence Could Strand the Most Expensive Capital Stock in History and Why Arriving Late may Yet become Europe's Advantage
abstract: This paper makes a forecast. The decisive economic threshold of the artificial-intelligence era will not be the arrival of superintelligence but the arrival of sufficiency: the point at which inexpensive, open-weight or locally deployable models can satisfy almost everything that most people and firms actually demand of them. Recent evidence on AI use shows that demand remains concentrated in practical guidance, information seeking, writing, learning and other bounded, readily verifiable tasks. If cheap models cross the sufficiency threshold, the frontier can keep advancing while the mass market stops paying to follow it. The forecast has a second half. The historic AI infrastructure build-out now under way - including roughly a trillion dollars of data-centre lease commitments that have not yet commenced, nearly four times the lease liabilities already recognised - is being contracted at scarcity-phase prices while financing the technological and organisational learning that makes each subsequent generation of equivalent capacity cheaper. If sufficiency arrives before that capital is amortised, late-deployed infrastructure can produce adequate intelligence at lower full cost than heterogeneous installed fleets. The resulting losses need not appear as the failure of the famous technology companies. They can surface first in the financing chain behind the build-out: lessors, special-purpose vehicles, specialised compute providers and their creditors, through lower utilisation, compressed returns, impairments and renegotiated commitments. The conjunction of demand-side sufficiency and a capital-vintage penalty creates a late-mover arbitrage, the regime written S_p > 1 and V > 1: an entrant no longer needs the best AI, only sufficient AI produced more cheaply. Applied to the European Union, this yields a conditional second chance. Europe's relatively younger future capital stock is an advantage only if it can mobilise capital, narrow its energy-cost disadvantage, preserve technological exit options and maintain the political capacity to act. The paper derives ten measurable forecasts and states explicit conditions under which its central hypothesis would be falsified.
why: AI sufficiency forecast; position paper.

title: Q-PORT: A Hybrid Quantum-based Portfolio Optimization Framework for Multiple Risk Profile with Turnover Control
abstract: The increasing connectivity of financial markets has accelerated information dissemination and heightened cross-market dependencies, making investment decisions more challenging. Portfolio optimization addresses this by balancing risk and return through optimal asset allocation. However, to the best of our knowledge, existing portfolio optimization methods do not support multiple investor risk profiles. Hence, different risk profiles require maintaining separate methods, increasing computational overhead and limiting scalability. Therefore, this paper proposes Q-PORT, a hybrid distributional reinforcement learning and quantum-based portfolio optimization framework that supports multiple investor risk profiles while incorporating portfolio turnover control. Specifically, Q-PORT employs an actor–critic implicit quantile network (AC-IQN) to learn a policy capable of generating portfolios for different risk profiles. This paper further introduces RATFormer, a novel neural architecture with a regime-adaptive tri-factor attention (RATFA) mechanism to learn regime-dependent representations from financial time series. To address the combinatorial asset selection problem, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm is employed to identify optimal asset subsets. Portfolio turnover is controlled through a minimum holding-period constraint (MHPC) that requires selected assets to remain in the portfolio for a minimum duration. The proposed Q-PORT framework is evaluated on NYSE and DJIA dataset for multiple risk profiles. The Q-PORT achieves Sharpe ratios of 2.1113, 1.2120, and 1.1038 on the NYSE, and 0.8999, 0.8579, and 0.7700 on the DJIA for the neutral, aggressive, and conservative investment profiles, respectively. These findings indicate that Q-PORT provides a scalable framework for personalized portfolio optimization, with decreased operational complexity while maintaining superior risk-adjusted performance.
why: Quantum portfolio optimization; not practical, no validation.

title: Can AI Outsmart Financial Fraud? A Critical Review of AI-Driven Fraud Detection, its Limitations, and the Need for Human Oversight
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used by banks, payment providers, insurers, and financial-technology firms to identify potentially fraudulent activity. Its value comes from the ability to examine high volumes of transaction, device, behavioural, and network data quickly. However, AI should not be viewed as a final solution to financial fraud. Fraudsters adapt rapidly, and generative AI has been made potent, impersonation, fake documentation, and social engineering cheaper and more convincing. This article considers whether AI can outsmart financial fraud. It argues that AI can improve prevention and investigation substantially when it is embedded within a wider framework of secure design, explainability, data governance, continuous monitoring, and meaningful human oversight. The discussion considers supervised learning, anomaly detection, behavioural analytics, graph-based methods, and natural-language processing, together with class imbalance, concept drift, false positives, bias, privacy, and adversarial threats. The conclusion is that AI does not remove fraud from the financial system; rather, it can make fraud harder to execute, less scalable, and more likely to be detected before significant loss occurs.
why: Fraud detection review; survey of existing approaches.

title: Dubstrata: A Cryptographically Verified Causal Knowledge Graph and Decentralised Prediction Market Microstructure Architecture for Forward-Looking Financial Risk Intelligence
abstract: Quantitative risk modelling in financial institutions has historically depended upon backwards-looking econometric models and statistical assumptions of stationarity that deteriorate during rapid macroeconomic regime shifts, geopolitical disruptions, and non-linear tail-risk shocks. Concurrently, decentralised prediction markets aggregate forward-looking collective intelligence with continuous state-contingent pricing, yet their direct utility for institutional risk systems remains impeded by thin-market illiquidity, Sybil manipulation, whale concentration, and unstructured narrative dispersion. Furthermore, emerging generative artificial intelligence and Large Language Model (LLM) narrative analysis tools frequently exhibit hallucinations, lack cryptographic grounding, and suffer from lookahead bias during quantitative backtesting.
why: On-chain risk prediction market architecture; very conceptual.

title: Competitive Automation Overshoot: Demand-Side and Capital-Composition Channels, with Market Concentration as a Moderator A Computational Comparison with Robustness Checks, Falsification Tests, and a Labor-Effort Hysteresis Extension
abstract: Firms adopting AI to substitute for labor face a coordination problem that recurs across two theoretically incompatible traditions: demand-side models, where aggregate demand depends on the same wage income that firms are cutting, and Marxian value-theoretic models, where the rate of profit depends on a capital-composition ratio that competitive automation drives in a self-undermining direction. We define a latent labor-intensity variable and channel-specific mappings into each tradition's own state variable, rather than assuming the two traditions share a state variable, and ask a narrower, computationally checkable question: under what conditions does decentralized, competitive automation converge on a labor intensity below the level that maximizes each channel's own aggregate outcome, a condition we call automation overshoot. Computed independently across a shared parameter space, the two channels show substantial but incomplete agreement (95% and 84% of the swept region show overshoot in the demand and Marxian channels respectively, 83% show it in both), a result that survives a fifteen-specification robustness check across alternative functional forms and internalization strengths (intersection fraction range 0.57-0.94, mean 0.82). Market concentration moves both channels toward less overshoot under fully independent native-parameter sampling that removes any shared coordinate system, a directional claim that survives four targeted falsification tests, one of which an earlier version of this model failed: a mechanical scale artifact in the demand channel, where more competing firms mechanically implied more aggregate automation activity regardless of any internalization behavior, is identified, derived away analytically, and corrected, with every result in this draft reported post-correction. A follow-up generalization addresses a further concern directly: firm count is not the same thing as market concentration. Removing the symmetric-firm assumption and re-deriving the demand channel's internalization term for heterogeneous market shares shows the correction scales as s_i^2 for each firm's own share s_i, so that aggregate internalization is governed by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, HHI = sum over i of s_i^2, with the earlier N-based results recovered as the symmetric-share special case. Holding firm count fixed at N=10 while redistributing shares from equal to one dominant firm moves demand-channel overshoot by a factor of 37; plotting demand-channel overshoot against HHI directly across firm counts from 5 to 50 collapses the resulting curves onto one relationship to within 5%, indicating HHI, not N, explains the concentration dependence in this channel substantially better than firm count alone, within the heterogeneous-share configurations tested and the isolating-benchmark design described in Section 4a. Separately, an analysis of the demand and Marxian channels' concentration relationships under independent sampling shows the two channels do not differ in "magnitude" on a single shared scale so much as in shape: the demand channel exhibits a sharp threshold effect concentrated at low firm counts, while the Marxian channel exhibits a shallow, gradual effect spread across the full sampled range of market structures. We extend the model with a hysteretic labor-effort function motivated by, but formalized independently of, Byung-Chul Han's account of the achievement subject: workers sustain effort under a belief that individual strategy can secure their position, a belief that collapses abruptly once a recognition threshold is crossed and recovers only past a lower threshold than the one that triggered the collapse. Wired into a simulated output trajectory, this produces a counterfactual output shortfall that persists after visible layoffs have already subsided; it is reported as an extension, not as co-equal with the core overshoot and concentration results.
why: Automation overshoot theory; pure computation, no empirical test.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Development of RegTech and SupTech: New Approaches to Financial Risk Management
abstract: Regulatory technology (RegTech) and supervisory technology (SupTech) have moved from experimental pilots to core infrastructure in financial oversight, with artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly embedded in compliance automation, anti-money laundering (AML) monitoring, anomaly detection, and predictive risk analytics.
