This paper examines how AI is reshaping the tools available to both regulated institutions and supervisory authorities, and how the pace and pattern of adoption differ between advanced economies and developing countries. Drawing on recent survey and policy work from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI), the World Bank, and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the paper argues that AI-enabled RegTech and SupTech offer significant gains in supervisory efficiency and risk detection, but that these gains are conditioned on data governance capacity, human capital, and the management of third-party technology dependencies. The paper concludes with a set of practical recommendations and a phased implementation roadmap for financial regulators.
why: RegTech/SupTech policy survey; not methods.

title: CELL Theory: Constrained Endosymbiotic Leadership and Logistics — A Cellular Metabolism Model of AI-Native Corporate Governance with the VITAL Assessment Framework
abstract: An AI system may produce useful drafts, classifications, recommendations, or reconciliations while an organization remains unable to delegate the operative decision. Traceability may be inadequate, sign-off non-delegable, authority boundaries unclear, the audit trail incomplete, or accountability unacceptable. CELLTheory,ConstrainedEndosymbioticLeadership &Logistics, addresses this problem as a function level governance model. Its core contribution is a constrained model of residual decision-authority allo cation; CELL supplies the architecture and vocabulary used to operationalize it. The model first applies categorical reservations and non-compensatory traceability and legitimacy floors within the VITAL as sessment of Viability, Integration, Traceability, Autonomy, and Legitimacy. Feasible assignments then compare the approved human process with recurring AI cost plus expected governance loss. Separate components characterize compute scaling and a Compliance Antibody Registry, defined as validated, retrievable control-memory rather than raw logging. The biological labels are mnemonics mapped to ob servable corporate objects and formal terms, not evidence that firms behave like cells. Three constructed sector cases illustrate the allocation rule; they are not observed cases or empirical tests. Validation is prospective and requires firm-function-period data capable of distinguishing prediction, within-function association, causal identification, and structural calibration. The analysis stops at function-level gover nance allocation; valuation and aggregate economic consequences require separate models and data.
why: AI governance decision model; framework not implemented.

title: Learned Optimization in Infrastructure Systems: A Survey of Methods and Deployment Patterns Across Energy, Finance, and Mobility
abstract: Machine learning and optimization methods have moved well beyond laboratory demonstrations and now operate inside production infrastructure of substantial economic and social consequence. This survey examines how these methods have been deployed-and what obstacles have been encounteredacross three sectors that together span a wide range of operational timescales and institutional contexts: cloud-hosted financial systems, grid-connected renewable energy installations, and long-horizon transportation infrastructure investment. Surveying recent literature, we find that reinforcement learning, multiobjective optimization, predictive anomaly detection, and datadriven planning tools have each found substantive application in all three domains, albeit against markedly different constraint profiles. Cloud financial infrastructure must contend with regulatory auditability requirements and asymmetric failure costs [1], [22]; photovoltaic grid integration faces data sparsity and adversarial cyber-physical threats [2], [19]; transportation funding optimization must balance revenue generation, spatial accessibility, and workforce equity simultaneously [3], [5]. Despite these differences, a coherent set of design principles emerges: careful state representation, conservative constraint encoding, and the alignment of optimization objectives with governance requirements are consistently more important than raw model capacity. We discuss shared failure modes, identify underexplored research directions including federated learning and crossdomain infrastructure linkage, and argue that interpretability is increasingly a technical prerequisite rather than an optional feature in regulated deployment settings.
why: Survey of infrastructure ML; rejects surveys, position papers, roadmaps.

title: The Entitlement Chain: Corporate Actions and Proxy in the U.S. Market — Why 2026 Broke Both Anchors, and What Comes Next
abstract: Corporate actions and proxy voting are conventionally treated as separate operational domains — staffed separately, systematized separately, and governed separately. This paper argues they are the same distribution problem solved twice: a single entitlement chain of five stages, running from issuer to beneficial owner, in which origination, canonicalization, position truth, instruction integrity and evidence must each hold for the outcome to be correct. That argument acquires urgency in 2026, when both halves of the chain lost their stabilizing anchor at once. On the corporate actions side, the ISO 20022 migration became a dated decommissioning schedule rather than a strategic choice, arriving alongside settlement compression that removed the buffer in which entitlement discrepancies were previously resolved. On the proxy side, the proxy-advisor benchmark policy is being unbundled, the largest index managers split their stewardship functions, and the SEC withdrew from substantive Rule 14a-8 no-action review — removing the neutral referee that made proposal exclusion predictable. Forecastability, not cost, became the scarce commodity. The paper introduces four original analytical frameworks: a five-layer Entitlement Chain Integrity model, an associated maturity model, a seven-class corporate actions failure taxonomy, and a five-component cost stack. It examines tokenized recordkeeping, pass-through voting, dual stewardship teams and agentic automation, and sets out playbooks by institution type. Written from two decades of practitioner experience in capital markets operations.
why: Corporate operations; entitlement chain is not quantitative finance.

title: Machine Learning Frameworks for Predictive Risk Management in Complex Business Systems
abstract: Business systems nowadays are becoming more and more interconnected via financial, operational, technological, supply-chain, customer, and digital networks, which results in risk situations that are marked by higher complexity, faster change, and greater uncertainty. In these kinds of situations, traditional methods of dealing with risk reactively may not be adequate since they typically detect threats only after the effects of those threats have already appeared, thereby making it necessary to use predictive approaches that can anticipate possible disruptions. Recent research has shown that artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and predictive analytics are being used more and more to enhance an organization's ability to identify risk, make forecasts, and assist in decision-making (Zeriouh and Amara, 2025; Tian et al., 2024; Fahrezi, 2024; Abdulla and Al-Alawi, 2024). This study looks at machine learning frameworks for predictive risk management in complex business systems, focusing on the way various ML methods contribute to risk identification, prediction, prioritization, and decision support. A literature-based methodology that is structured is used, involving systematic literature searching and the application of selection criteria, thematic synthesis, and a comparative analysis of the relevant studies. The results show that predictive analytics can help in the early detection of risk, supervised ML aids in the classification and prediction of risk, deep learning is able to capture complex nonlinear relationships, and anomaly-detection techniques enable continuous and real-time risk monitoring. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of ML is greatly affected by the quality of the data, the relevance to the context, the choice of model, interpretability, and the organization's level of readiness, meaning that there is no one framework that works well in all cases (Zeriouh and Amara, 2025; Tian et al., 2024). The study concludes that effective predictive risk management needs an integrated approach which combines complementary ML capabilities with continuous monitoring, human oversight, explainability, strong data governance, and adaptive learning. This kind of integration can improve an organization's preparedness and help it to respond more promptly, with greater knowledge and resilience, to risks as they emerge.
why: Literature review of predictive risk management frameworks.

title: Agentic AI: Technical Developments, Potential Impact on Consumers and Markets, and Regulatory Implications
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are beginning to change digital markets. Where earlier generative AI systems primarily produced text in response to prompts, agentic AI systems can plan tasks, use tools, retrieve information, maintain memory, coordinate workflows, and execute actions on behalf of users. This is turning AI from a passive information tool into a delegated intermediary between consumers, businesses and digital environments. Existing work on foundation models has provided important analysis of their inputs, development, partnerships, and potential concentration. This paper builds on that work but addresses a distinct, more recent evolution: the emergence of agentic AI as an operational ecosystem around foundation models. The paper contributes to the literature on agentic AI from a technical, economic and legal angle. First, it analyses technical developments in agentic AI. A strong technical understanding of agentic AI and its potential development is a necessary precondition for further analysis. Second, the paper identifies which consumer and market risks the rise of agentic AI may entail. A clear view of the underlying infrastructure, vendors, and emerging use cases helps do so. Third, the paper maps existing regulatory frameworks onto those consumer and market risks. The survey of consumer and market risks implies a wide range of potentially relevant instruments, including EU consumer law, the Digital Services Act (DSA), the Digital Markets Act (DMA), and competition law. Finally, the paper concludes with modest recommendations to drive the policy debate on agentic AI forward.
why: Agentic AI overview; survey/position paper format.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Portfolio Optimization and Algorithmic Trading: A Critical Survey
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is increasingly applied to algorithmic trading and portfolio optimization, motivated by its ability to learn a policy directly from data without a tractable model of price dynamics. This survey systematically reviews 124 papers published between 2018 and 2026, screened from an initial pool of 318 candidate records, and makes four contributions. First, it develops a taxonomy of Markov decision process (MDP) design choices, state space, action space, reward function, and environment dynamics, grounded in quantitative prevalence data across the corpus rather than narrative description alone. Second, it treats reward function design as a first-class analytical category: PnL-based rewards dominate (65 papers, 52.4%), followed by an other/heterogeneous residual category (19, 15.3%), multi-objective formulations (20, 16.1%), risk-adjusted rewards (16, 12.9%), and learned or self-adaptive formulations (4, 3.2%), and the survey synthesizes how these design choices relate to the trading behavior papers report. Third, it conducts a quantitative audit of evaluation methodology across the full corpus and finds systematic weaknesses: 86.3% of papers report an outperformance claim with no formal statistical test, 89.5% model no transaction costs or only a flat proportional fee, and, under a five-level maturity model this survey proposes, no paper in the corpus jointly satisfies realistic cost modeling, walkforward validation, a strong baseline, and multi-seed reporting, the minimum bar for a rigorous backtest rather than a proof of concept. Fourth, building directly on these findings, the survey identifies six open problems, non-stationarity and distribution shift, sample efficiency, the simulation-reality gap, riskconstrained optimization, interpretability, and offline reinforcement learning, and proposes concrete, adoptable methodological recommendations for closing them. The central conclusion is that the theoretical fit between DRL and trading is stronger than the field's current evidentiary standards support, and that closing this evaluation gap, not further algorithmic novelty, is the field's most consequential open problem.
why: DRL portfolio survey of 124 papers; literature review.

title: Algorithmic Autonomy and Responsibility Gaps: A Phenomenological Investigation of Accounting Professionals' Experiences with Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into accounting and auditing practices creates complex socio-technical challenges regarding professional identity, trust, and ethics, extending far beyond mere operational efficiency. While existing literature predominantly focuses on technology acceptance models and macroeconomic expectations, this study aims to deeply explore the lived experiences and ontological anxieties of Certified Public Accountants (CPAs) regarding AI technologies. Employing a descriptive phenomenological research design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 13 purposively sampled CPAs. The qualitative data were synthesized through a three-dimensional analytical matrix encompassing functional, emotional-cognitive, and ethical-professional dimensions. The findings reveal that while AI provides pragmatic benefits by reducing cognitive load, it simultaneously triggers risks of "automation bias" and professional alienation. Furthermore, the "black box" nature of machine learning algorithms and regulatory deficiencies lead to severe transparency crises and moral "responsibility gaps." The emotional ambivalence experienced by participants in the face of technological determinism proves that the profession is undergoing a profound ontological shift from traditional "bookkeeping" to strategic "data consultancy and ethical auditing." This study emphasizes that the "human-in-the-loop" principle is an ontological necessity for the sustainable integration of AI in the financial ecosystem. It provides strategic policy recommendations for professional organizations and regulators, including digital literacy upskilling, explainable AI (XAI) adoption, and intergenerational reverse mentoring.
why: Qualitative phenomenology; not quantitative.

title: Derivatives Trading Simulation Supported by AI
abstract: This paper presents an experiential learning framework that integrates artificial intelligence (AI) into a derivatives trading simulation implemented within a derivatives course, which is widely considered the most challenging course for undergraduate finance teaching. We employ the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) private trading challenge to improve students' comprehension of derivatives markets, investment decision-making, and report-writing skills. The derivatives simulation allows students to engage with real-time financial data and gain hands-on experience, fostering deeper learning of complex financial concepts. To ensure responsible teaching, we introduce a dual submission system where students submit their original and AI-assisted reports. This ensures academic integrity while allowing AI to support writing improvement. Our findings indicate that using AI-assisted tools enhances 42% of group projects to exceed writing expectations. We find that the original reports that meet grading expectations benefit more from AI-assisted tools than reports that are below expectations. The derivatives simulation significantly improves practical skills and critical thinking for students, while offering a replicable best practice for educators. By incorporating cutting-edge technology into finance education, our study provides a model for integrating experiential learning with AI tools to improve student outcomes in complex derivatives subjects.
why: Teaching framework; not research.

title: The Emerging EU Data Governance Framework under the European Data Strategy: From Regulating Rights to Regulating Markets
abstract: The European Union's rapidly expanding body of EU data law is undergoing a structural shift from a privacycentred data protection paradigm toward a comprehensive framework of data governance designed to regulate data life cycles, facilitate data flows, and support the creation of a single market for data. Drawing on the evolution from the Data Protection Directive to the GDPR and, subsequently, to the Data Strategy, the Data Governance Act, the Data Act, and the AI Act, the article shows how EU legislation increasingly targets the infrastructural, organizational, and governance conditions that enable data sharing across sectors while maintaining fundamental rights protections. We claim that the emerging, multi-instrument regulatory regime governing data access, sharing, markets, and social effects can best be understood through the paradigm of data governance, which is already well established in literature. We examine how new laws introduce cross-sectoral governance mechanisms, impose obligations on public and private actors for data availability, quality, integrity, and risk mitigation, and frame AI governance as inseparable from data governance. While identifying shortcomings-such as limited market analysis, procedural burdens, and unresolved tensions with existing privacy law-the article contends that these instruments collectively represent the EU's first meaningful attempt to regulate data flows as an economic resource and to build a coherent, risk-based data governance regime for the digital age.
why: Legal/regulatory survey on EU data governance.

title: Systemic Risk, Recommender Systems and Content Governance: The Digital Services Act and the Reinvention of Platform Regulation
abstract: the European Union's 2022/2065 concerning a Unified Market for Services on the Internet (the ’Digital Services in Academic Domains Act’ or ’DSA’) represents the most audacious European endeavor thus far to transcend the two-decade framework established by the Internet Commerce Directive and thereby redefine online intermediaries as proactive shapers of the online public sphere. This article examines the DSA's hierarchical framework of responsibilities, its preferential approach toward extremely large online spaces and search engines via the notion of 'systemic risk', its governance of machine learning recommendation systems and deceptive practices, and the nascent enactment actions of the European Commission, which is operating as a primary internet oversight body for the very first time. It argues that the DSA represents a fundamental rather than a gradual change in European platforms management, and its enduring significance will rely on how Articles 34 and 35 are practically interpreted by the Commission, the judiciary, and the appointed agencies. A formal segment establishes mathematical framework connecting the dynamics of recommended systems, virality thresholds, and the evaluation of systemic risk. The document concludes with five reformation objectives for the subsequent execution phase involving the DSA.
why: Legal analysis of EU Digital Services Act.

title: Certified envelopes for day-ahead cooling-side flexibility from liquid-cooled AI data-center thermal inertia in electricity markets
abstract: Artificial-intelligence computing is adding gigawatts of load to grids that now condition interconnection on flexibility. A liquid-cooled hall supplies it by letting its coolant warm, which cuts chiller power. Selling those cuts a day ahead is hard for two reasons. How deep a cut it can promise moves with tomorrow's humidity and workload, and a priced shortfall differs from a chip running too hot, which nothing pays for. This paper proposes ENCORE, Envelope-Certified Offering and Recourse. It computes the set of deliverable cuts, a polyhedron whose right-hand side moves with the dew-point forecast, then shrinks it by the worst case two calibrated disturbance sets admit, a wide one for chip safety and a narrow one for priced delivery, each calibrated per hour-of-day block at a level that tracks misses. A fixed-gain controller then delivers the offer, and on every hour the certificate covers it holds the chips safe and meets the metered whole-hour obligation. Across ten 2024 ERCOT weeks, on a causal price forecast and a stylized 30-minute reserve product, the hall commits 127 kW-h/day per megawatt of information-technology load and returns $7.45/MW-day with no hotspot violation on any covered hour, against an uncertified envelope that breaches the limit on 227 of 1,400 replayed day-and-seed combinations. Declaring an hour unavailable when its realized start sits outside the certified set turns down 104 of 190 calls and removes every failure and episode. No certificate break appears in four climates spanning 20 K of mean dew point, or across campuses of up to twenty halls.
why: Data center thermal flexibility; energy operations not finance.

title: AI Adoption and ESG Performance: A Bibliometric and Knowledge Mapping Review of Global Research (2010-2026)
abstract: AI is reshaping how organizations approach environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance, yet the scholarly literature examining this intersection remains fragmented. This study presents a bibliometric and knowledge mapping review of 1,959 publications from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus databases (2010-2026). Using a multidimensional methodological approach that combines performance analysis, co-word analysis, co-citation analysis, bibliographic coupling, co-authorship analysis, thematic evolution, thematic mapping, burst detection, and citation path analysis. We apply sophisticated Python-based analytics for bibliometric analysis and map the conceptual, intellectual, and social structures of this emerging field. Our findings reveal explosive growth beginning in 2020, with China, the United States, and the United Kingdom as the most prolific contributors. The conceptual landscape centers on seven distinct themes, anchored by artificial intelligence, ESG, machine learning, sustainability, and green innovation. Thematic evolution traces a clear progression from foundational discussions (2010-2015) toward applied AI-driven ESG applications (2021-2026). Emerging frontiers, including generative AI for ESG reporting, explainable AI in sustainability governance, and AI-enabled greenwashing detection, signal where the field is heading. We contribute an integrated theoretical framework bridging traditional strategic management theories with AI-specific perspectives, including algorithmic opacity and socio-technical systems theory. These findings offer a foundation for future scholarship and practical guidance for managers and policymakers navigating the intersection of AI and sustainability.
why: AI ESG bibliometric review; survey of literature.

title: Publication Benchmarking Data Based on Faculty Promoted at U.S. Institutions Among the Top 200 Accounting Research Institutions from 2020 to 2025
abstract: This paper provides publication benchmarking data for accounting faculty promoted to associate or full professor between 2020 and 2025 at 136 U.S. institutions ranked among the world's top 200 accounting research institutions. Grouping schools by research ranking, we use the 2025 ABDC Journal Quality List to report possible minimum publication hurdles and publication mixes across journal categories. Sensitivity analyses use alternative journal lists, including the top six accounting journals, byuaccounting.net, and the Financial Times Top 50. Because the sample spans the COVID-19 pandemic, we report time-to-promotion statistics, publication trajectories by years since Ph.D., and comparisons with prior benchmarking studies. The data also predate widespread use of generative artificial intelligence, providing a baseline for future comparisons for evaluating future publication records. Relative to faculty promoted from 2013 to 2019, minimum A* hurdles increased in most ranking groups for associate-professor promotion, while median time from Ph.D. to promotion lengthened to eight years.
why: Faculty promotion benchmarking data; no research finding

title: Reconciling AI, Gen Z, and "Just Pricing" for Planetary Bioeconomic Governance
abstract: Despite escalating evidence of climate extremes and warnings regarding the staggering costs of climate inaction, global capital allocation continues to prioritize defense, space exploration, and short-term accumulation over ecological engineering and biome protection. The central barrier to effective climate action is not a scarcity of technical solutions, but rather the structural alignment of political economy and technological deployment. Advanced engineering frameworks, such as Ultra-Reduced-Impact-Encased-Logging (URIEL) utilizing airborne robotics, demonstrate that selective timber harvesting can achieve near-zero canopy damage while remaining financially viable and socially inclusive. However, because technology is never politically neutral, the financial status quo prevents the widespread adoption of such innovations. Overcoming this institutional inertia requires a structural rupture driven by the convergence of Generation Z and Artificial Intelligence. Generation Z’s systemic environmental awareness and rejection of hyper-extractive labor models, combined with AI’s capacity to process complex socio-ecological data, enable dynamic models of "just pricing" (justum pretium). This economic framework integrates Hayekian market dynamics, Marxian surplus equity, and Lovelockian biophysical boundaries, directly embedding real-time ecological externalities into transaction costs to subsidize zero-impact operations. To prevent planetary collapse, public policy must overcome both technophobia and youth despondency. National governments and scientific institutions must actively establish tax-relieved bioeconomic zones, institutionalize open-source AI infrastructure for public procurement, and redirect strategic research funding away from offensive military expansion toward autonomous bioeconomic engineering. Harnessing AI alongside the ethical imperative of new generations offers a concrete pathway to reconcile economic vitality with long-term planetary survival.
why: Environmental manifesto; position paper.

title: Investing in Water: From Undervalued Common Good to Regulated Income -How Investors Can Take Part in the Fourth Megatrend
abstract: Water is the only economic good that nothing can replace-and at the same time one of the most underpriced. Four billion people experience severe water scarcity for at least one month a year, two-thirds of the world's river basins now carry too much or too little water, and with the data centres of artificial intelligence a new large consumer has arrived. This paper-the fourth of six on the great megatrends-examines the water megatrend from an investor's perspective: from hydrology through the economics of the value-price paradox to the investment programmes that regulators in Europe and America have already made binding.
why: Water investment theme commentary; not methods.

title: Nanozyme array from polydopamine-mediated carbon nanotubes and metal phthalocyanine derivatives for antibiotic sensing
abstract: The rapid and accurate identification of antibiotics in complex matrices remains a critical challenge. Nanozyme-based sensor array tackle rapid antibiotic identification in complex matrices via machine-learning-deconvoluted cross-reactive response patterns. Herein, we developed metal-nitrogen-carbon nanozymes from carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and metal phthalocyanines (MPc, Fe, Co, Cu) using polydopamine (PDA) as a mediator. PDA-coated CNTs improved CNT dispersion and anchored MPcs, pyrolysis yielded high-activity oxidase-like PDA@CNT/MPc nanozymes. A colorimetric sensor array based on three nanozymes generated unique antibiotic response fingerprints. Machine learning enables accurate classification of seven antibiotics in real samples and achieves a high discrimination accuracy. The integration of metal phthalocyanine-based nanozyme array with machine learning provides a rapid, portable, and high-throughput platform for antibiotic discrimination.
why: Nanozyme chemistry; completely off-topic.

title: Structure-Activity Relationship (SAR) Studies of Abaucin Derivatives Targeting the Lipoprotein Transport System in Acinetobacter baumannii
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) has been classified by the World Health Organization (WHO) as a critical priority antibiotic-resistant pathogen, making it one of the highest priorities for global antibiotic development. In 2023, abaucin, a narrow-spectrum antibiotic selectively targeting the lipoprotein transport system in Acinetobacter baumannii was identified through deep learning-based screening. In this study, we designed and synthesized 30 abaucin derivatives to further explore the structure-activity relationship (SAR). SAR analysis revealed that the spirocyclic scaffold, linker length and aromatic substituents played critical roles. Lead compound 28 was identified with markedly improved inhibition of LolF/D complex and antibacterial activity against A. baumannii (MIC = 0.5 μg/mL). Further studies demonstrated that compound 28 exhibited rapid and complete bactericidal kinetics and low prevalence of spontaneous drug resistance. Combination of compound 28 with a membrane permeabilizer PMB exhibited 100% protection in a mouse sepsis model. Compound 28 also showed satisfactory safety properties. Collectively, these findings highlighted compound 28 as a promising lead compound for the development of novel antibacterial agents against A. baumannii.
why: Organic chemistry; off-topic.

title: A dual-branch deep learning framework for site-to-pixel upscaling of in situ albedo measurements: Accounting for spatial heterogeneity and scale effects
abstract: Pixel-scale reference ”truth” serves as a critical link between in situ measurements and satellite observations. However, owing to surface heterogeneity, the upscaling of single-site observations to the satellite pixel scale has long been constrained by poorly understood mechanisms of heterogeneity effects, inadequate characterization of nonlinear responses, and insufficient utilization of spatial information. Existing methods, particularly machine learning approaches, generally adopt a direct point-to-pixel mapping strategy that implicitly assumes mutual independence among subpixels within a coarse pixel. This assumption conflicts with the spatial autocorrelation inherent in a spatially continuous land surface, thereby introducing systematic biases into upscaling results over heterogeneous land surfaces. To address this challenge, we propose a site-to-pixel upscaling method that integrates environmental attribute modeling with spatial context learning. The core of this method is a parallel dual-branch architecture comprising a multilayer deep neural network and a convolutional neural network. The former establishes a nonlinear mapping between environmental attributes and the target variable, whereas the latter extracts multiscale spatial heterogeneity patterns within the coarse pixel. The features from the two branches are then adaptively fused through a gating mechanism, followed by spatial aggregation using a point spread function. Evaluation across 416 globally distributed sites encompassing 15 land cover types shows that the model achieves R² values of 0.802–0.997 and RMSE values of 0.007–0.032. At sites jointly affected by spatial heterogeneity and topographic complexity, the median RMSE is more than 30% lower than that of the best-performing benchmark model. Ablation experiments show that the combined mechanism of per-subpixel modeling and residual learning is the primary source of model accuracy improvement, reducing RMSE by more than 60%. The complete dual-branch model accurately reproduces the spatial texture and spatial variability patterns within coarse pixels. Using MCD43A3 product validation as an example, the upscaled reference reduces validation RMSE by 10.2%–22.4%; at highly heterogeneous sites, Bias is reduced by 85.7%. This study demonstrates that the proposed method effectively enhances the ability of in situ observations to represent pixel-scale conditions over heterogeneous surfaces, providing a reliable and cost-effective solution for generating high-quality pixel-scale reference ”truth” and a fundamental basis for remote sensing product validation and the construction of pixel-scale training samples.
why: Satellite imagery albedo; environmental science off-topic.

title: Health Insurance Navigation Gaps in the United States
abstract: Background: Most working-age Americans carry health insurance, yet coverage and comprehension are not the same thing. Confusion about benefits, avoidance of needed care, and reliance on slow, fragmented workarounds remain common even among the insured. This study examines how adults in the United States actually experience the process of using their coverage, drawn from an original cross-sectional online survey. Methods: A convenience sample of 43 adults spanning a range of ages and insurance types completed a structured survey covering literacy confidence, care-avoidance behavior, frustration with existing tools, feature preferences, and current coping strategies. Results: Mean self-reported confidence in understanding one's benefits was 3.05 out of 5, and 34.9% of respondents placed their confidence at 2 or below. Close to half (44.2%) had delayed or skipped care because they were unsure what it would cost or whether it was covered. Deductibles and co-pays were the single largest source of frustration (53.5%), ahead of identifying in-network providers (46.5%). Over half of respondents (53.5%) said their main coping strategy was simply calling their provider or insurer, repeatedly. A striking 58.1% rated the need for a consolidated navigation tool at the maximum urgency level. The features respondents wanted most were benefit tracking (72.1%), cost forecasting (67.4%), and provider network comparison (51.2%). Conclusion: A measurable gap separates having insurance from being able to use it well. Respondents want an AI-driven benefits navigation tool that consolidates coverage data, forecasts costs, and points them toward both in-network providers and community care resources. These findings support building integrated digital navigation tools as a practical way to improve both healthcare access and consumer health literacy at once.
why: Health insurance navigation survey; off-topic.
